tips.title: German always says who
tips.body: In casual English you can sometimes skip the I, but German always says who is doing something. Bin on its own is not a sentence, but ich bin means I am. That is why the cards teach the person and the verb together: ich bin, du bist, er ist. Learn each pair as one chunk, and never leave out the ich, du or er when you speak.

examples.target: Er ist Max und sie ist Lena.

tips.title: Verbs change with who does them
tips.body: In German, the verb changes a little depending on who is doing it. The ending usually tells you who: -e for ich, -st for du and -t for er or sie, so ich habe, du hast, er hat. Möchte is the odd one: ich möchte and er möchte are the same, and only du gets an ending, du möchtest. When you speak, match the verb to the person, and when you listen, the ending helps you hear who it's about.

examples.target: Sie hat Kaffee und ich habe Wasser.
examples.en: She has coffee and I have water.

examples.target: Du möchtest Kaffee, und er möchte Wasser.
examples.en: You'd like coffee, and he'd like water.

tips.title: Every noun is der, die or das
tips.body: Every German noun is masculine, feminine or neuter, and the word for the shows which one: der, die or das. This applies to people and things alike: der Vater, die Mutter, das Haus, and even das Kind. You often can't guess it, so learn every noun with its der, die or das as part of the word. If you get the word right but use the wrong der, die or das, it counts as Nearly. Every noun also starts with a capital letter, wherever it is in the sentence.

tips.title: Den and einen: the accusative
tips.body: When a der word is the thing you have, want, see or order, the little word in front of it changes, and German calls this the accusative. Der becomes den and ein becomes einen: ich habe einen Bruder, or einen Kaffee, bitte. Mein works just like ein, so my father becomes meinen Vater. Die, das, eine and plurals never change, so eine Schwester and ein Wasser stay as they are. So when you order or say who you have, check whether the noun is a der word and add the -en.

tips.title: Questions start with the verb
tips.body: To ask a yes-or-no question, put the verb first: du bist müde means you are tired, and Bist du müde? means are you tired? English often adds do (do you have water?), but German simply moves the verb to the front: Hast du Wasser? With a question word like was, wer, wo, wann, wie or warum, the question word comes first and the verb comes straight after it. So Wo ist das Hotel? means where is the hotel, in the same order as English.

tips.title: Nicht and kein
tips.body: Nicht means not, so ich verstehe nicht means I don't understand. Before a noun that would have ein, or no article at all, German doesn't use nicht but says kein, which means not a or no. So ich spreche kein Deutsch means I don't speak German, and das ist kein Bier means that's not a beer. Kein takes the same endings as ein, so einen Bruder becomes keinen Bruder and eine Schwester becomes keine Schwester.

tips.title: Can, must, want: the second verb goes last
tips.body: Words like können (can), müssen (must), wollen (want) and möchten (would like) often team up with a second verb. The first verb changes with who does it, like ich kann or du kannst, and sits in its usual spot. The second verb goes to the very end of the sentence in its dictionary form, so ich möchte Wasser trinken means I would like to drink water. Everything else goes in between, and questions work the same way: Kannst du mir helfen? means can you help me? English says to drink or to help, but German needs no word for to here.

examples.en: I'd like to drink a coffee.

tips.title: Du and Sie
tips.body: German has two words for you: du for friends, family, children and people your age, and Sie for strangers, shop staff and officials. The polite Sie always has a capital S, even in the middle of a sentence. With Sie, the verb takes its dictionary form, just as it does with wir (we) and sie (they): Können Sie mir helfen? means can you help me? Sein (to be) is the exception, because you are is Sie sind. Ihr means you when you talk to several friends at once, but this app leaves its forms out.

tips.title: The verb comes second
tips.body: In a German statement, the verb always comes second. Second means the second part of the sentence, and a part can be one word like ich or a group of words like der Mann. You can start with the person, as in Ich gehe heute nach Hause, which means I'm going home today. If you start with something else, like a time or a place, the verb still comes second and the person moves behind it: Heute gehe ich nach Hause. So when you start with heute, morgen, jetzt or hier, put the verb next, then the person.

examples.en: Tomorrow Anna is going to Berlin.

tips.title: Verbs that split in two
tips.body: Some German verbs have a small front part that can break off: aufstehen (get up) is auf plus stehen. In an everyday sentence the front part jumps to the very end: Ich stehe früh auf means I get up early. Anrufen (call) works the same way: Ich rufe dich an means I'm calling you. In the dictionary form the verb stays in one piece, and after können or müssen it goes to the end in one piece too: Ich muss früh aufstehen. So when you hear a little word like auf or an at the end, join it back onto the verb to get the meaning.

examples.en: I have to get up early tomorrow.

tips.title: Liking: gern and mögen
tips.body: To say you like doing something, use the normal verb and put gern right after it: Ich trinke gern Kaffee means I like drinking coffee. To say you don't like doing it, put nicht before gern: Ich arbeite nicht gern means I don't like working. To like a thing or a person, use mögen, which is ich mag and du magst: Ich mag Musik means I like music. Ich möchte comes from mögen too, and it's the polite I would like, which is perfect for asking for things.

tips.title: Plurals have no single rule
tips.body: English mostly adds -s for more than one, but German plurals come in several patterns. Das Kind becomes die Kinder, die Frau becomes die Frauen, der Bruder becomes die Brüder, and das Hotel becomes die Hotels. Whether the noun is der, die or das, the word for the in the plural is always die. There's no rule you can rely on, so learn each plural together with its noun, and the answer on each card shows it to you. When you order, drinks often stay singular, so you say zwei Kaffee, bitte.

tips.title: After mit, bei and zu: the dative
tips.body: After mit (with), bei (at someone's place) and zu (to someone), the word for the or a changes, and this changed form is called the dative. Der and das become dem, die becomes der, and ein becomes einem or einer: mit dem Mann, mit der Frau, mit einem Kind. Mein changes just like ein, so you say mit meinem Vater and bei meiner Mutter. Ich becomes mir and du becomes dir, which is why you say mit mir and Wie geht es dir?

tips.title: Talking about the past: the Perfekt
tips.body: To talk about the past in conversation, German uses haben or sein plus a past form of the verb, and that past form goes at the end. Ich habe gearbeitet means I worked or I have worked, and ich bin nach Hause gegangen means I went home. Most verbs use haben, but verbs of moving or changing, like gehen, kommen and aufstehen, use sein. You don't have to guess which one: each verb's answer shows its past with the right helper, like hat gemacht or ist gegangen.

cards.trick: AN sounds like on: someone at the door is practically on it, knocking.

cards.hint: actual, existing in fact, as in real life; not echt, wahr, eigentlich or tatsächlich
cards.trick: WIRKLICH sounds like VIRK-likh, close to work-like: something that actually works in the world is real.

example.target: Mein Auto ist schon ziemlich alt.
example.en: My car is already pretty old.

cards.trick: ALT sounds almost like old said with a short a, and the two words share the same roots.
EINFACH, said EYEN-fakh, is literally onefold: you simply do one thing, no fuss, just do it.

example.target: Genau, das habe ich auch gedacht.
example.en: Exactly, that's what I thought too.

cards.trick: GENAU sounds like guh-NOW: the train leaves exactly NOW, right on the dot.

example.target: Frau Schmidt ist heute nicht da.

cards.trick: FRAU rhymes with how: how do you do, Mrs. Schmidt?

example.target: Kennst du den Weg zum Bahnhof?
example.en: Do you know the way to the station?

cards.trick: WEG, with a long e, sounds like vayk, close to way: der Weg is the way you walk.
cards.why: Der Weg (capital W, long e) is the way or path; lowercase weg means away or gone.

cards.hint: one more of the same, before ein
cards.trick: NOCH sounds like knock: knock on the bar for one more round.

example.target: Anna und Tom verkaufen ihr Auto.
example.en: Anna and Tom are selling their car.

cards.trick: IHR sounds like ear: the twins cover their ears.

cards.hint: to a place, as in take you home or take the kids to school (not mitnehmen)
cards.trick: BRINGEN sounds like bringing: Germans bring you home where English says they take you home.
cards.why: Use bringen for taking someone or something to a place; nehmen for taking hold of something or taking a bus.

cards.trick: FAHREN sounds like far-en: you drive a car when you need to go far.

example.target: Kannst du mal kurz meine Tasche halten?
example.en: Can you hold my bag for a second?

cards.trick: HALTEN starts like hold: to hold something is to halten it.

example.target: Ich warte im Auto auf dich.
example.en: I'll wait for you in the car.

cards.trick: IM sounds like the end of "him": squeeze "in dem" together and you get im, meaning "in the".

cards.hint: yes that contradicts a negative question

example.en: You're not hungry? Yes, I am!

cards.trick: DOCH ends in the throaty ch of Scottish loch, like a stubborn Scot insisting: oh yes it is!
cards.why: Use doch, not ja, to answer yes to a negative question or statement.

example.target: Guten Morgen! Hast du gut geschlafen?
example.en: Good morning! Did you sleep well?

cards.trick: MORGEN sounds a lot like "morning", and "Guten Morgen" is just "good morning".
cards.why: Use der Morgen, with a capital, for the morning; lowercase morgen means tomorrow.

example.en: Is that clear to you now?

cards.trick: KLAR sounds like clear said with a broad ah, klahr: something klar is clear.
PASSIEREN sounds like pass-SEE-ren: things that pass by right in front of you are things that happen.
VERSUCHEN sounds like fair-ZOO-khen: at the fair zoo, you try to feed the animals.
Ich DARF sounds like I dare: when you're allowed to, you dare to do it.
cards.why: Use dürfen when something is allowed; können when someone is able to do it.

example.en: Do you want tea or coffee?

cards.trick: ODER sounds like "other": this one or the other one.

cards.hint: not wrong; the everyday word, not korrekt
cards.trick: RICHTIG starts like a soft RIGHT: the German and English words share a root, and both mean correct.
NEU is said noy, rhyming with toy: a kid always wants a new toy.
FRAGEN (FRAH-gen) starts a bit like frog: picture a curious frog that asks everyone questions.
cards.why: Use fragen to ask a question; bitten to ask for something.

cards.trick: SICHER (ZIKH-er) is related to secure: a secure place is a safe place.

example.target: Nach dem Essen gehen wir spazieren.
example.en: After the meal we're going for a walk.

cards.trick: NACH sounds like "knock": after the film, someone knocks at the door.
HEISSEN sounds like "HY-sen", close to "Hi, son!": you greet someone by what they are called.

cards.hint: in the middle of doing it, not jetzt

example.target: Ich koche gerade, ruf mich später an.
example.en: I'm cooking right now, call me later.

cards.trick: GERADE sounds a bit like grade: I'm just grading papers right now, so don't interrupt.
cards.why: Use gerade for something going on at this very moment; jetzt for now in general.

cards.trick: ALS sounds a bit like "as" with an L slipped in: it works as "as".

example.target: Die Jacke steht dir echt gut.

cards.trick: STEHEN sounds like SHTAY-en, like stay in: clothes that suit you are ones you want to stay in.

example.en: I slept for a long time today.

cards.trick: LANGE sounds like long-uh: stretch the word long and it lasts a long time.
cards.why: Use lange for how long an action lasts; lang describes a long thing.

cards.trick: NICHTS sounds close to nix, the English slang word for nothing.
cards.why: Use nichts for nothing (not anything); nicht just says not.

cards.hint: as in to feel at ease, sich ... fühlen

example.target: Ich fühle mich hier total wohl.

cards.trick: WOHL is a cousin of English "well": when you feel wohl, you feel well and at ease.
LETZTE sounds like LETS-tuh, as in let's: let's go, this is the last one.
MAN sounds almost like English man: any man at all, meaning one, you, or people in general.
cards.why: Use man, lower case with one n, for people in general; der Mann is a man.

cards.trick: GLEICH sounds like the end of alike, glye-ch: things that are alike are the same.
MAL sounds like mall: two times three shops in a mall makes six.

example.target: Ich helfe ihnen morgen beim Umzug.

cards.trick: IHNEN sounds like "EE-nen": they're in need, so you give help to them.
cards.why: Lowercase ihnen means (to) them; capitalised Ihnen is the polite (to) you.

cards.hint: as in you're right, used with haben

example.target: Du hast recht, das war mein Fehler.
example.en: You're right, that was my mistake.

cards.trick: RECHT is a cousin of English right: the German ch sound matches the old gh in right, so you have recht means you're right.

example.target: Die beiden sind ein schönes Paar.
example.en: The two of them are a lovely couple.

cards.trick: PAAR sounds a lot like the English pair, and it means a pair or a couple.

cards.hint: the full word, not the casual was

example.en: Do you want something to drink?

cards.trick: ETWAS sounds like ET was: ET was something strange from outer space.

cards.hint: moving outward, as in get out!
cards.trick: RAUS rhymes with house: get out of the house!
MENSCH sounds like the English word mensch, borrowed from Yiddish: a mensch is a good human being.

example.target: Ich wohne nicht mehr in Berlin.
example.en: I don't live in Berlin anymore.

cards.trick: MEHR sounds like "mare": the old mare doesn't run anymore, she's nicht mehr racing.

example.target: Der Ritter hat den Drachen getötet.

cards.trick: TÖTEN sounds a bit like toting: someone toting a gun is ready to kill.
cards.why: Töten is the standard, neutral word for kill; umbringen is the more everyday spoken one.

cards.hint: a light or device, not on
cards.trick: AUS sounds close to out: lights out means the lights are off.

example.target: Dein Bruder ist ganz schön groß.

cards.trick: GROSS sounds like gross: a tall guy has grown to a gross size, a full head above everyone else.

example.target: Mein Opa ist letztes Jahr gestorben.

cards.trick: STERBEN (SHTAIR-ben) is a cousin of English starve: starve long enough and you die.

cards.hint: to sum up or draw a conclusion, not so

example.en: So, what are we doing now?

cards.trick: ALSO, said AL-zo, is a false friend: it never means also, it means so, and it even ends in the sound so.
cards.why: Use also for 'so' when summing up; for English 'also, too' say auch.

example.target: Wir sitzen alle um den Tisch.
example.en: We're all sitting around the table.

cards.trick: UM sounds like "oom": picture people humming "oom" as they walk in a circle around something.

example.target: Erzähl mir, was gestern passiert ist!

cards.trick: ErZÄHLen sounds like air-TSAY-len, and that TSAYL is close to tale: you tell a tale.
NAME is spelled just like English name and means the same; Germans just say it NAH-muh.
UNSER starts with uns, German for us, so unser is what belongs to us: our.

cards.hint: a situation or investigation, not a container

example.target: Die Polizei hat den Fall gelöst.

cards.trick: FALL rhymes with pal: your detective pal falls onto a new case every week.

cards.hint: one everyday verb, of a fact or statement, not a person (Stimmt! = that's true)

example.target: Stimmt, das hast du mir schon gesagt.
example.en: Right, you already told me that.

cards.trick: STIMMEN sounds like shtim-men, close to chime in: you chime in with Stimmt! when something is right.
cards.why: Use stimmen when a fact or statement is right; use recht haben when a person is right.

cards.en: I'll wait [in front of] the cinema

example.target: Ich warte vor dem Kino auf dich.
example.en: I'll wait for you in front of the cinema.

cards.trick: VOR sounds like fore, as in the fore of a ship: the part in front.

cards.hint: to receive (the standard everyday word, not kriegen or erhalten)
cards.trick: BEKOMMEN sounds like become but is a false friend: it means to get, like getting a present that comes to you.
NACHT is a cousin of night: its ch, said like the throaty sound in Scottish loch, sits where English night has its silent gh.

example.target: Spielst du heute mit uns Fußball?
example.en: Are you playing soccer with us today?

cards.trick: SPIELEN starts like SHPEEL, a salesman's spiel: he plays a little act to win you over.

cards.hint: toward me, with movement: come here (the short word, not hier or hierher)
cards.trick: HER sounds like hair: come here so I can fix your hair.
cards.why: Use her for movement toward you (Komm her!); hier for where something is (Ich bin hier).

cards.trick: SUCHEN sounds like zoo-ken: picture Ken looking for his lost keys all over the zoo.

cards.hint: by car, bus, train or bike, not on foot

example.target: Wir fahren morgen mit dem Zug nach Berlin.
example.en: We're going to Berlin by train tomorrow.

cards.trick: FAHREN sounds like fare: you pay a fare when you go somewhere by bus or train.
cards.why: Use fahren when you go by car, bus, train or bike; use gehen when you go on foot.

cards.hint: of a bus or train making its scheduled stop at a station (one word, not anhalten)

example.target: Der Bus hält direkt vor meinem Haus.
example.en: The bus stops right outside my house.

cards.trick: HALTEN contains halt, as in English: a bus that comes to a halt stops.
cards.why: Use halten when a bus, train or car stops; use aufhören when you stop doing something.

cards.trick: LOS sounds like loose: when something has come loose, you ask what's wrong.
DOCH rhymes with Scottish loch: you swore you'd never visit Loch Ness, but you went after all.

example.target: Ich hole dir ein Glas Wasser.
example.en: I'll get you a glass of water.

cards.trick: HOLEN sounds like haul in: you go off and haul something back in, which is fetching it.

example.en: Are you coming along? Of course!

cards.trick: KLAR sounds like clear: when the answer is clear, you just say of course.

cards.hint: running at an easy pace or as exercise, not rennen (sprint)

example.target: Ich laufe jeden Morgen fünf Kilometer.
example.en: I run five kilometers every morning.

cards.trick: LAUF sounds a bit like lope (LOWF): to lope is to run with long, easy strides.
cards.why: Use laufen for running or jogging at an easy pace; rennen for dashing or sprinting.

example.target: Ich bleibe heute zu Hause, denn ich bin müde.
example.en: I'm staying home today because I'm tired.

cards.trick: DENN sounds like a fox's den: I stayed in my den because I was tired.
cards.why: After denn the verb stays second; after weil it goes to the end.

cards.trick: SCHNELL sounds like "snail" with a sh, and a snail is anything but fast.

cards.hint: tag at the end, the word that also means or
cards.trick: ODER sounds like "or...?": you're coming, or not? That trailing question means right?

cards.hint: before an adjective, as in really good; the word that also means right, not wirklich, echt or sehr
cards.trick: RICHTIG sounds a bit like RIGHT, and English says right good too: right good means really good.
cards.why: Use richtig before an adjective to mean very (richtig gut); wirklich means truly.

cards.hint: looks like naturally; not klar or selbstverständlich
cards.trick: NATÜRLICH sounds like naturally, and in English naturally also means of course.
cards.why: Natürlich is the all-purpose 'of course'; klar is the short, casual reply among friends.

example.en: I have to go to the doctor tomorrow.

cards.trick: ZUM sounds like zoom: you zoom to the doctor or to the station.
cards.why: Use zum (zu + dem) before der- and das-words; zur (zu + der) before die-words.

cards.trick: TOT sounds like tote: after the battle, soldiers tote the dead away.
cards.why: Tot is the adjective dead; der Tod, with a d, is the noun death.

example.target: Es ist schon zehn nach drei.

cards.trick: NACH sounds like "knock": the clock knocks ten minutes past three.

cards.hint: of words, as in what does that word mean; not bedeuten or meinen
cards.trick: HEISST sounds like "Hi, Ist": a word says hi and tells you its name, which is what it means.
cards.why: Use heißen for what a word means (Was heißt das?); meinen is what a person means.

cards.trick: GERADE ends like parade: a parade marches in a straight line.

cards.en: [when] I was little, I had a dog

example.target: Als ich klein war, hatte ich einen Hund.
example.en: When I was little, I had a dog.

cards.trick: ALS sounds like "Al's": back when Al's dog was a puppy, one time in the past.
cards.why: Use als for one time in the past; wenn for repeated or future events.

cards.hint: you all, informal, as the object
cards.trick: EUCH sounds like OYCH, like shouting Oi! at a group: oi, I mean you lot.
cards.why: Use euch for several friends as the object; dich for one friend.

cards.trick: VerDAMMT sounds like "fair damned", and it means damned; on its own, Verdammt! is like shouting Damn!

example.target: Der Junge spielt im Garten Fußball.
example.en: The boy is playing football in the garden.

cards.trick: JUNGE sounds like YOUNG-uh: a young one in the family is the boy.

example.target: Die Lampe ist über dem Tisch.
example.en: The lamp is over the table.

cards.trick: ÜBER sounds like Uber, and a flying Uber would zoom right over your head.

example.target: Ich treffe heute Abend meine Freunde.

cards.trick: TREFFEN sounds like "traffic in": you meet your friends in the busy traffic of town.
cards.why: Use treffen for meeting up with someone; kennenlernen for meeting someone for the first time.

example.target: Stell die Flasche auf den Tisch.
example.en: Put the bottle on the table.

cards.trick: STELLEN sounds like "shtell", close to "stall": you put a horse standing up in its stall.
cards.why: Use stellen for putting something down upright; legen for laying it down flat.

cards.hint: very soon, within a minute or two; not sofort or bald

example.en: Wait a second, I'll be right there!

cards.trick: GLEICH sounds a bit like glide: I'll glide over to you in a moment.

example.en: The others are already waiting outside.

cards.trick: ANDERE sounds a bit like another: another one is the other one.

example.target: Guten Tag, wie geht es Ihnen?

cards.trick: IHNEN sounds like "EE-nen": a polite "you" for a stranger who isn't in your inner circle.
cards.why: Use Ihnen, always capitalised, for a polite 'you' after verbs like helfen; use dir with friends.

cards.hint: the side, before a noun: the right hand
cards.trick: RECHT sounds close to right with a breathy ch: think of the right hand you write with.
cards.why: Use recht with an ending before a noun (die rechte Hand); use rechts alone to say where something is.

cards.hint: call out, send for; not on the phone
cards.trick: RUFEN sounds like ROOF-en: you climb on the roof and call out to everyone below.
cards.why: Use rufen to call out or send for someone; use anrufen to phone them.

cards.hint: also a matter, an affair; not Ding

example.target: Pack deine Sachen ein, wir fahren gleich.
example.en: Pack your things, we're leaving soon.

cards.trick: SACHE starts like English sack: you stuff all your things into a sack.
cards.why: Use Sache for things in general, belongings and matters; Ding is a casual word for a physical object.

cards.trick: AM sounds like the English am, and you see it in the morning too: am Morgen means in the morning.

cards.hint: in that place, away from here, not da
cards.trick: DORT rhymes with fort: the fort is over there, far away.
cards.why: Use dort for a place clearly over there, away from you; da is the shorter everyday word for there.

cards.hint: as in keep going, go on

example.target: Mach einfach weiter, du schaffst das!
example.en: Just keep going, you can do it!

cards.trick: WEITER sounds like VY-ter, close to fighter: a fighter never stops and keeps going on, further and further.

cards.hint: sends the verb to the end

example.target: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich krank bin.
example.en: I'm staying home because I'm sick.

cards.trick: WEIL sounds like vile: I stayed in because the weather was vile.
cards.why: Weil sends the verb to the end; denn also means because but keeps the verb second.

cards.hint: adjective, as in the first day

example.target: Das ist mein erster Tag hier.
example.en: This is my first day here.

cards.trick: ERSTE sounds like AIR-stuh, as in the old English word erstwhile: erst once meant at first, earliest.
cards.why: Use erste before a noun (mein erster Tag); for doing something first, use erst or zuerst.

cards.trick: VERGESSEN sounds like fair GUESSin': once you forget something, all you can do is guess.
JEDER sounds like "yay, there": you cheer every time, for every single one.

example.target: Kein Problem, ich helfe dir gern.
example.en: No problem, I'm happy to help you.

cards.trick: PROBLEM sounds just like English problem, only stressed at the end: pro-BLAYM.

cards.en: I'm saving [in order to] buy a car
cards.hint: used with zu before the verb

example.target: Ich spare, um ein Auto zu kaufen.
example.en: I'm saving in order to buy a car.

cards.trick: UM ... ZU sounds like "oom ... tsoo": um, to do that, you need a plan.

example.target: Meine Mutter liebt Ordnung im Haus.
example.en: My mother loves order in the house.

cards.trick: ORDNUNG starts like 'order': when everything is in order, it's tidy.

cards.hint: polite title before a man's surname
cards.trick: HERR sounds like hair: Mr. Smith always combs his hair before work.

cards.en: I'm telling you [so that] you know
cards.hint: purpose, verb goes to the end

example.target: Ich sage es dir, damit du Bescheid weißt.
example.en: I'm telling you so that you know.

cards.trick: DAMIT sounds like "dam it": you build a dam so that the water stays put.
cards.why: Use damit when a new subject follows; use um ... zu when the same person does both things.

example.target: Ich zeige dir morgen die Stadt.
example.en: I'll show you the city tomorrow.

cards.trick: ZEIGEN sounds like TSY-gen, a bit like sign: a sign shows you the way.

example.en: The girl is playing in the garden.

cards.trick: MÄDCHEN sounds like MAID-shen, a little maiden: a girl.

cards.en: I was in Berlin two years [ago]

example.target: Ich war vor zwei Jahren in Berlin.
example.en: I was in Berlin two years ago.

cards.trick: VOR sounds like fore, as in before: vor zwei Jahren is two years before now, so two years ago.

example.target: Ich will heute Abend allein sein.
example.en: I want to be alone tonight.

cards.trick: ALLEIN sounds like "a line": a line with only you in it means you are alone.
JEMAND sounds like "yay, man!": you shout it when someone finally shows up.

example.target: Was ist das für ein Ding?
example.en: What kind of thing is that?

cards.trick: DING sounds like thing said with a d: that thing on the door goes ding.
cards.why: Use Ding for a physical object; Sache also covers matters and affairs.

cards.hint: at the end, with sein: that's long ago (not vor)

example.en: That was a long time ago.

cards.trick: HER sounds like hair: when you still had all your hair was long ago.
cards.why: Use her at the end with sein (Das ist lange her); vor before the time (vor zwei Jahren).

cards.hint: what a person means, not a word

example.en: What do you mean by that?

cards.trick: MEINEN starts like "mine": what you mean is what's in your own mind, so mine-en means to mean.
cards.why: Use meinen for what a person means; bedeuten for what a word or thing means.

cards.hint: the word that also means now

example.target: Nun, das ist eine gute Frage.

cards.trick: NUN sounds like noon: well, it's noon, so let's start talking.

cards.hint: have an opinion of, used with von

example.target: Was hältst du von meinem neuen Freund?
example.en: What do you think of my new boyfriend?

cards.trick: HALTEN sounds like hold: what opinion do you hold of it?

cards.hint: short everyday word, as in come in

example.target: Komm rein, die Tür ist offen.
example.en: Come in, the door is open.

cards.trick: REIN rhymes with fine: come on in, it's fine!

cards.hint: particle stressing something obvious, with a note of reproach (not ja, not a tag like oder)
cards.trick: DOCH sounds like a sharp Scottish loch with a d: a quick, impatient sound for something everyone knows already.
BIS sounds like the start of biscuit: you have to wait until the biscuits are done.

example.target: Ich sorge dafür, dass alles klappt.
example.en: I'll make sure everything works out.

cards.trick: SORGEN (ZOR-gen) starts like Zorro, who always makes sure justice gets done.

example.target: Wir laufen nach Hause, es ist nicht weit.
example.en: We're walking home, it's not far.

regional.text: gehen (laufen there usually means to run)

cards.trick: LAUFEN (LOW-fen) sounds like loafin': loafing around town on foot means walking.
cards.why: Use laufen when you stress going on foot; gehen is the general word for going.

cards.hint: the little word in questions, not dann
cards.trick: DENN sounds like English then, as in a curious question: what's up, then?
cards.why: Use denn in questions to sound curious; dann means then in the sense of next or after that.

cards.hint: casual opener for a greeting, two letters, not so or also
cards.trick: NA sounds like a relaxed nah, but Germans use it like well or so to start a casual chat.
cards.why: Use na to casually open a chat or a question; use also to sum up or draw a conclusion.

cards.trick: WELT sounds like veldt, the wide open plains of Africa; picture the whole world as one giant veldt.

cards.hint: one word: zu + der, before a die-word
cards.trick: ZUR sounds like "tsoor": it is zu (to) with the r of der stuck on, so it means to the.
cards.why: Use zur before die-words (zur Arbeit); zum before der and das words (zum Arzt).

cards.trick: NATÜRLICH starts with Natur, which sounds like nature: what comes from nature is natural.
VERLIEREN sounds like "fair LEER-en": when a game isn't fair, you leer at the winner because you lose.
TOLL rhymes with British doll: getting a great new doll is awesome!

cards.hint: starting from a time, not von

example.en: From Monday on, I'm working again.

cards.trick: AB sounds like "up": from Monday UP onward, everything starts from that point.
cards.why: Use ab for a starting point from now on; von for who or where something comes from.

example.target: Die Hose ist mir zu weit.
example.en: These trousers are too loose on me.

cards.trick: WEIT sounds like "vite", a lot like "wide": baggy trousers are wide and roomy.
JUNG sounds almost like young, because German says j like y: a young person is jung.

example.target: Er ist wohl schon zu Hause.

cards.trick: WOHL sounds like "vole": if the garden has holes, there's probably a vole.

example.target: Wir gehen heute zusammen ins Kino.
example.en: We're going to the cinema together today.

cards.trick: ZUSAMMEN sounds like tsoo-ZAH-men, close to to summon: you summon your friends so you're all together.

cards.hint: be lying down or located, not tell a lie

example.target: Dein Handy liegt auf dem Tisch.
example.en: Your phone is lying on the table.

cards.trick: LIEGEN sounds like LEE-gen, a cousin of English lie: picture yourself lying on a beach in the lee of a dune.
cards.why: Use liegen when something is lying somewhere; legen when you put it down flat.

cards.trick: DURCH sounds like "doorch", close to "door": you walk through a door.

example.target: Wir reden später über das Problem.
example.en: We'll talk about the problem later.

cards.trick: ÜBER sounds like Uber, a company everyone loves to talk about.

example.target: Der Ball hat mich am Kopf getroffen.
example.en: The ball hit me on the head.

cards.trick: TRIFFT sounds like "tripped": the arrow never tripped up and hit the target dead center.

cards.hint: the verb used with eine Frage, not fragen

example.target: Darf ich dir eine Frage stellen?
example.en: Can I ask you a question?

cards.trick: STELLEN sounds like "shtell", close to "tell": you tell someone your question by putting it in front of them.
cards.why: Use stellen with eine Frage (eine Frage stellen); fragen asks on its own.

cards.trick: ECHT sounds a bit like act: if it's no act, it's real.

example.target: Weißt du, ob Anna heute kommt?
example.en: Do you know if Anna is coming today?

cards.trick: OB sounds like 'up', as in 'it's up in the air' whether it will happen or not.
cards.why: Use ob for 'if' meaning whether (after know, ask); wenn for 'if' as a condition.

cards.hint: before a noun, as in the best friend
cards.trick: BESTE sounds like BEST-uh: it is just English best with a little uh on the end.

example.target: Die Toilette ist da hinten rechts.
example.en: The toilet is back there on the right.

cards.trick: RECHTS sounds like wrecks: all the wrecked cars are parked on the right side of the road.
cards.why: Use rechts on its own for where something is (da rechts); before a noun it is recht with an ending.

cards.trick: HAND sounds almost like English hand, just with a broader ah and a final t sound: it means the same thing.

example.target: Ich brauche noch ein paar Minuten.
example.en: I need a few more minutes.

cards.trick: EIN PAAR sounds like a pair: a pair is two, and a few is just a little more than that.
cards.why: Lowercase ein paar means a few; capitalised das Paar means a couple or pair of two.

example.target: Ich fühle mich heute viel besser.

cards.trick: FÜHLEN sounds close to "feel-en": the ü is an ee said with rounded lips, so you can almost hear feel in it.

cards.hint: to make it, succeed at something

example.en: Don't worry, you can do it!

cards.trick: SCHAFFEN sounds like 'shove on': keep shoving on and you'll manage it in the end.

cards.hint: talking to two or more friends
cards.trick: EUER sounds like OY-er: shout Oi! at a group of friends and ask whether that dog is yours.
cards.why: Use euer for your when talking to two or more friends; dein for one friend.

cards.trick: WAHR sounds like VAR, football's video referee, which checks what is true.
WIESO sounds like "vee-zo" and is wie (how) plus so: "how so?" is just another way to ask why.
cards.why: Wieso is the casual, chatty why; warum is the standard word that fits everywhere.

example.target: Du musst an der Tür ziehen, nicht drücken.
example.en: You have to pull the door, not push.

cards.trick: ZIEHEN, said TSEE-en, is a distant cousin of tug and tow: when you tug or tow something, you pull it.
JEDER sounds like "YAY-der": everyone in the room shouts yay.
cards.why: Use jeder for everyone, with a singular verb (jeder weiß); alle means all of them and takes a plural verb (alle wissen).

cards.hint: personally, the standard word; not selber, allein or mich
cards.trick: SELBST sounds like a squashed "self": it adds -self, as in myself, yourself, himself.
cards.why: Use selbst for doing something yourself; use mich or sich when you are the object of the verb.

cards.hint: looks like the English word, not Augenblick

example.target: Warte einen Moment, ich komme gleich!
example.en: Wait a moment, I'm coming right away!

cards.trick: MOMENT is the English word moment, just stressed at the end: mo-MENT.

example.target: Ist bei dir alles in Ordnung?

cards.trick: IN ORDNUNG sounds like 'in order': if things are in order, they're okay.

cards.hint: polite word for a man, as in ladies and gentlemen

example.target: Der Herr da drüben möchte zahlen.
example.en: The gentleman over there would like to pay.

cards.trick: HERR sounds like hair: a true gentleman never has a hair out of place.

example.en: What are you doing with it?

cards.trick: DAMIT is da plus mit, "there-with": with that thing there.

cards.hint: direct your eyes, as in look out the window; not gucken, sehen or aussehen
cards.trick: SCHAUEN sounds like "SHOW-en": when someone shows you something, you look.
GENUG sounds like "guh-NOOK": once every nook is stuffed full, you have enough.

example.target: Vor dem Essen wäschst du dir die Hände.
example.en: You wash your hands before dinner.

cards.trick: VOR sounds like the fore in before: something that comes vor dinner comes before it.
cards.why: Use vor before a noun (vor dem Essen); bevor starts a clause with its own verb.

example.en: What are you getting for your birthday?

cards.trick: KRIEGEN sounds like KREE-gun: agree to a gain and you get something.
cards.why: Use kriegen in casual speech; bekommen is the neutral word for writing and polite talk.

example.target: Ich trinke meinen Kaffee ohne Zucker.
example.en: I drink my coffee without sugar.

cards.trick: OHNE sounds like "oh, nah": oh, nah, I'll go without it.
SCHLAFEN sounds like "shh, loafin'": hush, I'm loafing in bed and about to sleep.
FAMILIE sounds like fa-MEE-lee-uh, just English family with one extra syllable at the end.

cards.hint: give your opinion, as in Was ___st du? (what do you reckon?); not denken, glauben or finden

example.target: Ich meine, wir sollten jetzt gehen.
example.en: I think we should go now.

cards.trick: MEINEN sounds like "mine-en": you say what's on your mind, your own opinion, when you think something.
BEIDE sounds like "BY-duh": picture both twins waving bye at once.

example.target: Das Kind ist schon wieder gefallen.

cards.trick: FALLEN sounds just like English fallen, and the meaning is the same: to fall.
REIN sounds like Rhine, the river: imagine its water clean and pure.

cards.hint: with sich, not sitzen or hinsetzen

example.en: Come and sit down with us!

cards.trick: SETZEN sounds like "sets in": you set yourself into a chair and sit down.
cards.why: Use sich setzen for the act of sitting down; sitzen for being seated.

cards.hint: the German sigh word with a throaty ch, as in ... so

example.target: Ach so, jetzt verstehe ich das.
example.en: Oh, I see, now I understand.

cards.trick: ACH sounds like a throaty ah, the sigh you let out when something suddenly makes sense.

cards.hint: one verb with sich and um
cards.trick: SORGEN (ZOR-gen) sounds like sore again: worrying leaves your head sore again.

cards.hint: how things are going, as in how's it going at work? (not gehen or klappen)
cards.trick: LAUFEN also means run, and English says things are running smoothly when they go well.

cards.hint: one-word command shouted by police or guards, not Stopp
cards.trick: HALT is the English halt, as a guard shouts: Halt, who goes there?

cards.hint: short word before nicht, not überhaupt
cards.trick: GAR rhymes with far: gar nicht means not at all, far from it.
NÄCHSTE sounds close to 'next', with a soft hissing ch in place of the x: the next one.

example.en: I don't have much time today.

cards.trick: WENIG starts with a sound like vain: a vain person shares very little with others.

example.target: Komm, wir gehen heute Abend ins Kino.
example.en: Come on, let's go to the movies tonight.

cards.trick: INS sounds like English in's, a squeezed in + das: you go ins Bett, into the bed.
cards.why: Use ins for going into a place; im for being in it.

example.target: Mein Sohn ist sechs Jahre alt.
example.en: My son is six years old.

cards.trick: SOHN sounds like zone and looks like son: your son is in the zone when he plays.
ERINNERN has inner in it: to remember, you look into your inner mind and find the past.
cards.why: Use sich erinnern to remember something yourself; erinnern without sich means to remind someone.

cards.trick: NIEMAND sounds like "knee mant": think "no man" standing there, so nobody at all.

cards.hint: what you call a loved one, the everyday word (not Liebling)

example.target: Schatz, kommst du heute Abend mit?
example.en: Honey, are you coming along tonight?

cards.trick: SCHATZ sounds like "shots": your honey is the one person you'd take a shot for.

example.target: Ich warte seit Montag auf deine Antwort.
example.en: I've been waiting for your answer since Monday.

cards.trick: SEIT sounds like "site" said with a buzzy z: you've been stuck on this site since Monday.

example.target: Ich warte schon seit einer Stunde.
example.en: I've been waiting for an hour.

cards.trick: STUNDE sounds like SHTUN-duh, close to stunned: waiting a whole hour left me stunned.
SOFORT sounds like zo-FORT: the enemy is coming, so run back to the fort immediately!

example.en: Will you excuse me for a moment?

cards.trick: The middle of entSCHULDigen sounds like "should": you should excuse someone who says sorry for their fault (Schuld).

cards.en: I'm just coming back [from the] doctor

example.en: I'm just coming from the doctor.

cards.trick: VOM is said like fom, close to from: vom means from the.

example.target: Ich war nur einmal in Berlin.
example.en: I've only been to Berlin once.

cards.trick: EINMAL sounds like "ein meal": ein means one, so one meal is something you eat just once.

example.en: Do you want some of it?

cards.trick: DAVON, said dah-FON, is da (there) plus von (of, from), so it literally means of that, which is of it.

example.target: Die Jacke passt mir nicht mehr.
example.en: The jacket doesn't fit me anymore.

cards.trick: PASSEN sounds like passing: a key that passes smoothly into the lock fits.
cards.why: Use passen when clothes are the right size; stehen when they look good on someone.

cards.hint: casual, before an adjective; the word that also means genuine
cards.trick: ECHT sounds a bit like act: no act, I really mean it.
cards.why: Use echt in casual talk before an adjective; wirklich is the neutral word for really.

example.target: Danke dafür, das war echt nett.
example.en: Thanks for that, that was really nice.

cards.trick: DAFÜR sounds like dah-FUER: DA means there or that and FÜR sounds a bit like for, so it means for that.

example.target: Nächste Woche fahre ich nach Berlin.
example.en: Next week I'm going to Berlin.

cards.trick: WOCHE sounds like VOKH-uh, a bit like vodka without the d: picture a week-long party with seven days of vodka.

cards.hint: said of a person, as in I'm done (with my work)

example.target: Ich bin mit den Hausaufgaben fertig.

cards.trick: FERTIG sounds like "fair tick": the last box gets its fair tick once the job is finished.

example.target: Ich bin wegen der Arbeit hier.

cards.trick: WEGEN sounds like VAY-gen, close to wagon: we were late because of the wagon that broke down.
cards.why: Use wegen before a noun (wegen der Arbeit); weil starts a clause with a verb.

example.en: I've got something in my eye.

cards.trick: AUGE sounds like OW-guh: you yell ow when something gets in your eye.

cards.hint: the short word for movement there, away from you (not dahin, dorthin, dort or da)
cards.trick: HIN sounds like "in" with an h: picture yourself heading in over there, moving away from where you stand.
cards.why: Use hin for movement there, away from you; da or dort for where something is.

cards.hint: bring into being, as in creating jobs or making room; not erschaffen, kreieren or erstellen

example.target: Er hat etwas ganz Neues geschaffen.

cards.trick: SCHAFFEN sounds a bit like 'shaping': when you shape something new, you create it.

example.target: Das Wetter ist heute echt schlecht.
example.en: The weather is really bad today.

cards.trick: SCHLECHT sounds a bit like "slacked": work that somebody slacked on is bad work.
cards.why: Use schlecht for poor quality, the opposite of gut; schlimm for something serious or awful.

example.target: Ich bin in fünf Minuten da.
example.en: I'll be there in five minutes.

cards.trick: MINUTE sounds like "mee-NOO-tuh", nearly the English "minute" with an extra syllable at the end.

example.en: Which bus goes to the station?

cards.trick: WELCHER is an old cousin of English which: drop the -er ending and welch- looks a lot like which.

cards.hint: to another city, with nach; the short verb, not umziehen

example.target: Wir ziehen nächstes Jahr nach Berlin.
example.en: We're moving to Berlin next year.

cards.trick: ZIEHEN, said TSEE-en, is how you pull your whole life along with you when you move to a new city.
EINZIG starts with ein, German for one: the only one there is, just one single thing.
cards.why: Use einzig for the only one of something (meine einzige Chance); use nur for merely or just.

cards.hint: the word that also means -self, not sogar
cards.trick: SELBST sounds like "self": even the man himself knows it, so selbst also means even.
WICHTIG sounds roughly like VISH-tish: your most important wish always goes at the top of the list.

example.target: Die Katze schläft unter dem Tisch.
example.en: The cat is sleeping under the table.

cards.trick: UNTER sounds almost exactly like English under, just with a t in place of the d.

example.target: Mein Schlüssel ist schon wieder verschwunden.

cards.trick: verSCHWINden sounds like fair SHVIN-dlin, a swindling: after the swindle, the crook and your money disappear.

cards.hint: give someone a name, not phone
cards.trick: NENNEN sounds a bit like naming: when you name someone, you call them something.
cards.why: Use nennen for calling someone a name; anrufen for phoning, rufen for calling out.

example.target: Ich schicke dir gleich die Adresse.
example.en: I'll send you the address in a moment.

cards.trick: SCHICKEN sounds like "shicken", almost "chicken": picture yourself sending a chicken through the post.
HOCH sounds a bit like hawk: a hawk flies high in the sky.

cards.hint: only so far, also not until; not nur
cards.trick: ERST sounds like first without the f: at eight the day has only just begun.
cards.why: Use erst for only so far or not until (time); nur for only meaning merely, just.

cards.trick: NETT sounds like "net": a nice, kind friend is your safety net when you fall.

example.target: Bist du verrückt? Das ist viel zu gefährlich!
example.en: Are you crazy? That's way too dangerous!

cards.trick: VERRÜCKT sounds like fair-wrecked: a mind that is fairly wrecked has gone crazy.

regional.text: In Switzerland people commonly say das Bébé.

cards.trick: BABY is borrowed straight from English and sounds the same: a baby is a baby, it just takes das.
HOFFEN starts like hope with an f in place of the p: you hope with your fingers crossed.
GEGEN sounds like GAY-gun, a lot like the start of again-st: you stand against something again and again.

cards.hint: the noun, as in many thanks

example.en: Thanks a lot for your help!

cards.trick: DANK sounds like thank said with a D at the start: vielen Dank means many thanks.
cards.why: Say danke on its own to thank someone; der Dank is the noun, used in phrases like vielen Dank.

cards.trick: LIEBER sounds like LEE-ber, close to old English liefer, as in I had liefer go: I would rather go.
cards.why: Use lieber for what you prefer (I'd rather); eher for what is more likely (more like).

cards.hint: in length or time, not height
cards.trick: KURZ sounds like curt: a curt reply is a short one.

cards.hint: seat someone, place a bet (the putting that goes with sitzen)

example.target: Ich setze zehn Euro auf Rot.
example.en: I'm putting ten euros on red.

cards.trick: SETZEN starts like "sets": you set something in its place.

example.target: Beeil dich, sonst kommen wir zu spät.
example.en: Hurry up, otherwise we'll be late.

cards.trick: SONST sounds like zonst, close to zones: stay inside the safe zones, otherwise you're in trouble.

example.target: Der Film hat ein trauriges Ende.
example.en: The movie has a sad ending.

cards.trick: ENDE sounds like EN-duh, just the English word end with a little uh tacked onto the end.
KOPF sounds like "cop" with a puff at the end: a cop wears his helmet on his head.

cards.hint: the everyday word, as in I don't care
cards.trick: EGAL sounds like ay-GAHL, close to equal: when both options are equal, it doesn't matter which.

cards.hint: the everyday word, as in what do you actually want? (not tatsächlich)

example.en: What are you actually doing here?

cards.trick: EIGENTLICH sounds like eye-gent-lish: keep an eye on that gent, he is actually a spy.

cards.hint: shrugging particle, one word: it can't be helped (not eben, einfach or nun mal)

example.target: Das ist halt so, da kann man nichts machen.
example.en: That's just how it is, there's nothing you can do.

cards.trick: HALT sounds like English halt: the argument halts there, because that's just how it is.

cards.hint: a place or a person, not gehen

example.target: Er verlässt das Haus um acht.
example.en: He leaves the house at eight.

cards.trick: VERLASSEN sounds like "fair lass, then...": the fair lass left him and walked out the door.

cards.en: Do you have your phone [on you]?
cards.hint: one word, having it with you

example.en: I don't have any money on me.

cards.trick: DABEI sounds like "dah-BY": the thing is right there by you, so you have it on you.

example.target: Dein Auto steht vor dem Haus.
example.en: Your car is parked in front of the house.

cards.trick: AUTO sounds like OW-toe, short for automobile: an automobile is a car.

example.target: Erinnere mich morgen an den Termin.
example.en: Remind me about the appointment tomorrow.

cards.trick: ERINNERN has inner in it: to remind someone is to poke their inner memory.
cards.why: Use erinnern without sich to remind someone; with sich (sich erinnern) it means to remember.

example.target: Ich sitze im Auto und warte auf dich.
example.en: I'm sitting in the car, waiting for you.

cards.trick: SITZEN sounds like "zits in": a teen sits in his room staring at his zits.
cards.why: Use sitzen for being seated; sich setzen for the moment you sit down.

example.en: The pirates are looking for the treasure.

cards.trick: SCHATZ sounds like "shots": pirates fire shots to guard their buried treasure.

cards.hint: a time that is still going on

example.target: Ich wohne seit zwei Jahren hier.
example.en: I've lived here for two years.

cards.trick: SEIT sounds like "sight" with a z: no end in sight, it's been going on for years.
cards.why: Use seit for a time that is still going on now; für for a set length of time, often one that is planned.

cards.trick: UHR sounds a lot like hour: a clock or watch tells you the hour.

example.target: Ruf mich an, bevor du gehst.

cards.trick: BEVOR sounds like buh-FOR, almost exactly the English word before.
cards.why: Use bevor before a whole clause with its own verb; use vor before a noun (vor dem Essen).

cards.trick: The middle of entSCHULDigen sounds like "should": when it's your fault (Schuld), you should apologize.

example.target: Ich schreibe dir später eine Nachricht.
example.en: I'll write you a message later.

cards.trick: SCHREIBEN sounds like SHRY-ben, close to scribe: a scribe is someone who writes.

example.en: I'm at the doctor's right now.

cards.trick: BEIM sounds like by 'im: you're by him, at the doctor's.

example.target: Bist du bereit? Wir gehen gleich los.
example.en: Are you ready? We're leaving in a minute.

cards.trick: BEREIT sounds like "be right": I'll be right there, I'm ready!
cards.why: Use bereit for prepared or willing; fertig for finished, done with something.

cards.hint: be convenient, as in that works for me

example.en: Does Monday at eight work for you?

cards.trick: PASSEN sounds like pass: a plan that suits you gets a pass, so you say passt!

cards.hint: informal, a man you don't know; the word that also means type (not Kerl)

example.target: Wer ist der Typ da drüben?

cards.trick: TYP is spelled like type minus the e: some guy is just a certain type of man.

example.target: Ich habe einen guten Grund dafür.
example.en: I have a good reason for it.

cards.trick: GRUND sounds like ground, said groont: the grounds for doing something are your reason.
DARÜBER is da (there) plus über (about): talking about there, about that thing, means talking about it.

cards.hint: ready to go because you've finished getting ready (the word that also means finished, not bereit)

example.target: Bist du fertig? Wir müssen los.
example.en: Are you ready? We have to go.

cards.trick: FERTIG sounds like "fair tick": every item on your list has its tick, so you're ready to go.
cards.why: Use fertig for all set to go or done; bereit for prepared or willing to do something.

cards.trick: FALSCH sounds like "false" with a soft "sh" at the end: a false answer is a wrong answer.
TÜR sounds like a pouty "door" with a T at the front, and the two words are related: knock on the Tür.

example.target: Keine Sorge, das ist nicht so schlimm.
example.en: Don't worry, it's not that bad.

cards.trick: SCHLIMM sounds like "slim": when your chances are slim, things are looking bad.
cards.why: Use schlimm for something serious or awful; use schlecht for poor quality, the opposite of good.

example.en: What do you say to that?

cards.trick: DAZU (dah-TSOO) is da plus zu, like old English thereto: to that.
SCHWER sounds like shvair, close to swear: lifting something heavy makes you swear.

cards.hint: everyday word, as in that's enough!
cards.trick: REICHEN sounds a bit like reaching: once the money reaches the price, it is enough.
DARAN sounds like dah-RAHN, there-on: your thoughts are fixed on it, so you think of it.

cards.hint: to be pleasing to someone: das ___ mir
cards.trick: GEFALLEN sounds like "guh-FAHL-en", like "go fall in" love: whatever you fall for is something you like.
cards.why: Use gefallen when the liked thing is the subject (Das gefällt mir); mögen when you are (Ich mag das).

cards.hint: da- + auf; also means on it

example.en: I'm already looking forward to it.

cards.trick: DA-RAUF sounds like there, a roof: something sitting there on a roof is on it.

example.target: Viel Glück morgen bei der Prüfung!
example.en: Good luck with the exam tomorrow!

cards.trick: GLÜCK sounds a bit like glue: good luck sticks to you like glue.

cards.en: you can [go ahead and] sit down
cards.hint: particle meaning feel free, no need to hesitate
cards.trick: RUHIG starts like roo: a calm roo tells you to relax and go ahead, no need to worry.
UNTER sounds like under: if you're among a crowd, you're under its cover.
SPÄTER sounds like "shpay-ter", close to "shape it later": you'll shape it later, not now.

example.en: What are you reading right now?

cards.trick: LESEN sounds like lazin': lazin' on the sofa, you read a good book.

example.target: Ich habe noch einige Fragen an dich.
example.en: I still have a few questions for you.

cards.trick: EINIGE starts with EIN (one): one, then a few more join in, and you have some.
cards.why: Einige is the neutral word for a few; ein paar is the casual everyday way to say it.

example.target: Du hast mir das Leben gerettet!

cards.trick: RETTEN sounds like "red ten": ten firefighters in red rush in to save you from danger.
ERST sounds like first with the f dropped, and it means first.
WORT sounds like "vort", which is just English "word" with a v sound in front and a hard t at the end.

example.target: Die Katze schläft hinter dem Sofa.
example.en: The cat is sleeping behind the sofa.

cards.trick: HINTER sounds like hinder or hind, as in an animal's hind legs, which come behind.

cards.hint: what a word or thing signifies
cards.trick: BEDEUTEN sounds like "buh-DOY-ten": a bed at ten, and you know what that means: bedtime.
cards.why: Use bedeuten for what a word or thing means; meinen for what a person means.

example.target: Bis bald, ich ruf dich an!
example.en: See you soon, I'll call you!

cards.trick: BALD sounds like "bahlt", close to English bald: worry this much and you'll be bald soon.

example.target: Ich bin gegen acht zu Hause.

cards.trick: GEGEN sounds like GAY-gun: the gun goes off around eight, give or take a few minutes.
cards.why: Use gegen for a rough time (around eight); um for an exact clock time (at eight).

example.target: Wasch die Gabel ab, da ist noch Ketchup dran.
example.en: Wash the fork, there's still ketchup on it.

cards.trick: DRAN sounds like drawn on: something drawn on a page is stuck right on it.

example.target: Du scheinst heute müde zu sein.

cards.trick: SCHEINEN sounds like shining: a shiny surface only seems to be gold until you look closer.
KURZ sounds like curt: keep it curt, just a quick moment.

cards.en: I'm tired, [that's why] I'm going home

example.target: Ich bin müde, darum gehe ich ins Bett.
example.en: I'm tired, that's why I'm going to bed.

cards.trick: DARUM sounds like "da room": the room was a mess, that's why I left da room.
SONST sounds like zonst, close to zones: once you've seen these zones, what else is there?
cards.why: Use sonst for anything else besides this; use noch for one more of the same.

example.target: Der Kerl da drüben starrt dich an.
example.en: That guy over there is staring at you.

cards.trick: KERL sounds like curl: picture a tough guy with one big curl hanging over his forehead.
cards.why: Kerl is a bit rougher and folksier, as in fellow or bloke; Typ is the neutral casual word for a guy you don't know.

cards.trick: IDEE sounds like ee-DAY, almost the English word idea, which is exactly what it means.
cards.why: Use Idee for a plan or thought you have; for 'no idea' (no clue) say keine Ahnung.

cards.hint: the first word of the pair, before mehr
cards.trick: JE sounds like yeah: yeah, the more the merrier!

cards.hint: before a noun, as in the actual reason behind it; the same word as actually (not wahr, echt or tatsächlich)
cards.trick: EIGENTLICH sounds like eye-gent-lish: under his disguise, the gent's real face shows in his eyes.

example.en: Put the weapon down right now!

cards.trick: WAFFE, said VAFF-uh, is a cousin of English weapon: the p of weapon became ff in German.
SICH VERLASSEN sounds like "fair lass": a fair, loyal lass is someone you can rely on.

example.target: Wir gehen heute schwimmen, bist du dabei?
example.en: We're going swimming today, are you in?

cards.trick: DABEI sounds like "dah-BY": I'll be right there by your side, so count me in.

example.target: Kannst du die Tasche für mich tragen?
example.en: Can you carry the bag for me?

cards.trick: TRAH-gen sounds like drag: when a bag is too heavy to carry, you drag it.
ÜBERHAUPT starts like Uber: I don't need an Uber at all, I'll walk.

example.target: Ich habe keine Angst vor dem Tod.

cards.trick: TOD sounds like toad: the toad on the busy road met its death.
FANGEN starts with the sound of fang: a snake uses its fangs to catch its prey.

example.target: Ich wohne seit einem Monat in Berlin.
example.en: I've been living in Berlin for a month.

cards.trick: MONAT, said MOH-naht, is close to moon and month: a month is about one trip of the moon around the earth.

cards.hint: telling the time, as in three o'clock

example.target: Wir treffen uns um drei Uhr.

cards.trick: UHR sounds like hour: drei Uhr is the third hour, three o'clock.
cards.why: Use Uhr for the time on the clock (drei Uhr); use Stunde for an hour as a length of time.

cards.hint: the particle; not halt or einfach

regional.text: halt is the usual particle here and in Switzerland (Das ist halt so); eben in this sense sounds northern German.

cards.trick: EBEN sounds like even: it's even, flat, no way around it, that's just how it is.

cards.hint: as in no idea, a clue; not Idee

example.target: Keine Ahnung, wo mein Handy ist.
example.en: No idea where my phone is.

cards.trick: AHNUNG sounds like a shrug: Ah, noong... ah, no idea!
cards.why: Use Ahnung for having a clue (keine Ahnung); use Idee for an idea you come up with.

cards.trick: VOLL sounds like "foll", close to "full": a full glass is voll.

cards.hint: one word before a noun: bei + dem

example.target: Beim Essen schaue ich gern Serien.
example.en: I like watching shows while eating.

cards.trick: BEIM rhymes with time: at the time you're doing something.

cards.en: I'm tired, [that's why] I'm staying home
cards.hint: one word starting with des-, not darum or deswegen

example.target: Ich bin müde, deshalb bleibe ich zu Hause.
example.en: I'm tired, so I'm staying home.

cards.trick: DESHALB sounds like dess-halp: I'm lost, that's why I need help.
cards.why: Deshalb, darum and deswegen all mean that's why; deshalb is the neutral everyday choice, with the verb right after it.

example.target: Ich lege die Schlüssel auf den Tisch.
example.en: I'm putting the keys on the table.

cards.trick: LEGEN sounds like LAY-gun: you lay the gun down flat on the table.
cards.why: Use legen for putting something down flat; stellen for setting it upright.

cards.trick: TYP looks like type without the final e, and it means type too.

example.target: Ich sitze zwischen Anna und Tom.
example.en: I'm sitting between Anna and Tom.

cards.trick: ZWISCHEN sounds like tsvish-en: picture a ball that goes swish right between two goalposts.

cards.en: the table, and the lamp [above it]

example.target: Da ist die Tür, und darüber hängt eine Uhr.
example.en: There's the door, and a clock hangs above it.

cards.trick: DARÜBER is da (there, it) plus über, which sounds a bit like over: over it, above it.
POLIZEI (po-lee-TSAI) sounds like police plus eye: the police keep an eye on you.

cards.hint: not genuine, as in a fake name

example.target: Er hat einen falschen Namen benutzt.

cards.trick: FALSCH sounds like "false-sh": false teeth and a false name are fake ones.

example.target: Während des Films habe ich geschlafen.

cards.trick: WÄHREND sounds like "where end": during a long film you keep asking where the end is.

example.target: Ich kümmere mich um den Hund.
example.en: I'll take care of the dog.

cards.trick: KÜMMERN sounds a bit like come in: come in, and I'll take care of you.

example.en: Do you want fries with it?

cards.trick: DAZU (dah-TSOO) sounds like there, too: fries come along there, too, on the side.
SCHWER sounds like shvair, close to swear: a hard task makes you swear.

cards.hint: hand something to someone, a bit more polite than geben (not geben or rübergeben)

example.target: Reichst du mir mal das Salz?
example.en: Can you pass me the salt?

cards.trick: REICHEN sounds like reaching: you reach across the table to pass someone the salt.

cards.hint: where you are, not out of
cards.trick: DRAUSSEN sounds like drowsin': you lie drowsin' outside in the sun.

example.target: Kannst du mir einen Gefallen tun?
example.en: Can you do me a favor?

cards.trick: Der GEFALLEN sounds like "guh-FAHL-en": a friend who has fallen in a hole needs a favor to get out.

example.target: Meine Tochter ist gerade fünf geworden.

cards.trick: TOCHTER, said TOKH-ter, sounds like a rough "daughter", and the two words share the same old root.
GLÜCK starts with the same gl sound as glee, and glee is pure happiness.

cards.hint: peaceful, not only low in volume
cards.trick: RUHIG starts like roo: picture a sleeping kangaroo, a roo lying calm and quiet.

example.target: Als Kind war ich ziemlich arm.
example.en: I was pretty poor as a kid.

cards.trick: ARM sounds like English arm: a poor beggar holds out an arm for a coin.

cards.en: [according to] the weather report, it'll rain
cards.hint: one short word, with no article after it here (not nach or gemäß)

example.en: According to the weather report, it'll rain tomorrow.

cards.trick: LAUT, the word for loud: whatever a source says out loud is what things are according to.

example.target: Ich hätte gern ein eigenes Zimmer.
example.en: I'd like a room of my own.

cards.trick: EIGEN sounds like "EYE-gun": your own eye, your own gun, things that belong to you alone.
FAST looks like English fast, but it means almost: run fast and you're almost there.

example.target: Das ist derselbe Typ wie gestern.
example.en: That's the same guy as yesterday.

cards.trick: DERSELBE has SELBE in it, close to English self: the thing itself again, the very same one.
cards.why: Use derselbe for the very same one; gleich for things that are alike.

example.target: Ich verspreche dir, ich komme zurück.
example.en: I promise you I'll come back.

cards.trick: VERSPRECHEN sounds like fair-SHPREKH-en, holding sprechen (to speak): to promise is to speak your word fairly.

example.en: I don't like people like that.

cards.trick: SOLCHER begins with so, and German says ZOL-kher: things that are so this way are such things.

cards.hint: movement downward, the short everyday word, as in come down (not herunter or nach unten)
cards.trick: RUNTER sounds like "roon-ter": picture a stone rune tumbling down the stairs.
cards.why: Use runter for moving down; unten for where something is (downstairs, below).

example.target: Er hat mich ins Gesicht geschlagen.
example.en: He hit me in the face.

cards.trick: SCHLAGEN sounds like slug: to slug someone is to hit them hard.
WEN, said like vain, ends in N the way whom ends in M: both are the object form of who.
cards.why: Use wen when who is the object (whom); use wer when who is the one doing it.

cards.trick: GESCHICHTE sounds like the verb geschehen, to happen: a story tells you what happened.

cards.en: there's the table, put the box [on it]

example.target: Da ist der Tisch, stell die Kiste drauf.
example.en: There's the table, put the box on it.

cards.trick: DRAUF ends in AUF, said like "owf", the German word for on, so drauf means on it.
cards.why: Drauf is the casual spoken short form of darauf; use darauf in careful speech or writing.

cards.trick: SCHEIN sounds just like shine, and that's what the sun does: die Sonne scheint.

cards.hint: adjective, as in the back door
cards.trick: HINTER sounds like hinder or hind: a horse's hind legs are its back legs.

cards.hint: any old thing, informal; not etwas
cards.trick: IRGENDWAS ends in was, said vass, which means what, so irgend-what is some-what-or-other: anything at all.

cards.hint: finished, as in the movie is over (not aus or fertig)
cards.trick: VORBEI sounds like for bye: when the party is over, it is time for bye.

cards.hint: after a not: but rather, not aber

example.target: Ich komme nicht heute, sondern morgen.
example.en: I'm not coming today, but tomorrow.

cards.trick: SONDERN sounds like sunder, to split apart: it splits off the wrong idea, not this but that.
cards.why: Use sondern after a not to give the right alternative instead; aber is the ordinary but.

cards.trick: JOB is the English word job borrowed, said the same way, just with the final b sounding like a p.
cards.why: Use der Job for a job you hold; die Arbeit for work in general or going to work.

cards.trick: HERZ sounds like "hearts" said quickly, ending in a ts sound: your heart is in your chest.

example.en: Where are you going this summer?

cards.trick: WOHIN sounds like voh-HIN: wo means where, and hin sounds like heading in, so it asks where you are heading.
cards.why: Use wohin to ask where someone is going; use wo to ask where someone or something is.

cards.hint: fairly, before an adjective; not ganz

example.target: Das Essen hier ist ziemlich teuer.
example.en: The food here is pretty expensive.

cards.trick: ZIEMLICH sounds like TSEEM-lish, close to seemly: it seems pretty good, quite fine.
DRAN sounds like drawn: your name has been drawn, so you're up and it's your turn.

example.target: Alle sind schon da außer Max.
example.en: Everyone is already here except Max.

cards.trick: AUSSER sounds like OW-ser, close to outer: the one on the outer edge is left out, everyone except him.

example.target: Du trägst heute eine schöne Jacke.
example.en: You're wearing a nice jacket today.

cards.trick: TRAH-gen sounds a bit like dragon: picture a dragon wearing a big winter coat.

cards.hint: in a question, the word that also means at all; not eigentlich or sowieso

example.en: What are you doing here anyway?

cards.trick: ÜBERHAUPT sounds like Uber, how: Uber, how did you even get here anyway?

example.en: Which country would you like to visit?

cards.trick: LAND sounds like 'lant', almost English land: a country is a big piece of land with borders.

cards.hint: a one-syllable resigned shrug (not na ja or the German also)
cards.trick: TJA sounds like a short sigh, tyah, the noise you make with a shrug before saying well, what can you do.

example.target: Es ist schon spät, ich gehe ins Bett.
example.en: It's already late, I'm going to bed.

cards.trick: SPÄT sounds like shpate: a spate of late nights leaves you tired.

example.en: Why are you laughing so loudly?

cards.trick: LACHEN sounds like LAUGH with a throaty ch on the end, and that's because the two words are cousins: to laugh.

cards.en: I'm tired, [that's why] I'm staying home
cards.hint: the one built on wegen, not deshalb or darum

example.target: Ich bin müde, deswegen bleibe ich zu Hause.
example.en: I'm tired, that's why I'm staying home.

cards.trick: DES-VAY-gen ends in wegen, which means because of, so deswegen is because of that: that's why.
cards.why: Deswegen, deshalb and darum all mean that's why and can swap freely; deswegen is the one built on wegen.

example.en: I just need some peace and quiet.

cards.trick: RUHE sounds like ROO-eh: a kangaroo napping in the shade, finally enjoying some peace and quiet.

cards.hint: casual slang before an adjective, the same word as full
cards.trick: VOLL sounds like "full": something voll gut is good to the full, totally good.

example.target: Ich habe eine Frage an dich.
example.en: I have a question for you.

cards.trick: FRAGE sounds like "FRAH-guh", a bit like "fog": a question is something you ask when you're in a fog.

cards.hint: paired with aber later in the sentence

example.target: Das Auto ist zwar alt, aber es fährt.
example.en: The car is old, sure, but it runs.

cards.trick: ZWAR sounds a bit like a quick 'sure': sure, it's old, but it still runs.
DRIN sounds like the start of drink: the drink is in there, inside the glass.

example.en: My dad is going to kill me!

cards.trick: UMBRINGEN sounds like oom-bringing: think of bringing someone down to the ground, which in a crime film means to kill them.
cards.why: Use umbringen in everyday talk; töten is the plainer, more formal word for kill.

cards.hint: the short word, not meistens or normalerweise

example.target: Ich fahre meist mit dem Rad zur Arbeit.

cards.trick: MEIST rhymes with iced, and starts with the M of most: in summer, most drinks are iced.

cards.hint: to seem, as in sounds good; one word, not sich anhören
cards.trick: KLINGEN sounds like clinking: clinking glasses make a bright sound.

cards.hint: as in even my dad, not selbst
cards.trick: SOGAR sounds like zo-GAR, close to so far: she went so far, she even quit her job.
cards.why: Sogar only ever means even; selbst can mean even too, but mostly means -self.

cards.en: I brush my teeth [after] I've eaten

example.target: Ich putze mir die Zähne, nachdem ich gegessen habe.
example.en: I brush my teeth after I've eaten.

cards.trick: NACHDEM sounds like 'knock them': only after you knock them on the door do they open.
cards.why: Use nachdem before a whole clause (after I've eaten); use nach before a noun (nach dem Film).

cards.trick: WÄHREND sounds like "where end": while you wait, you wonder where the end is.

cards.hint: to risk it, not sich trauen

example.target: Ich wage es nicht, ihn zu fragen.
example.en: I don't dare to ask him.

cards.trick: WAGEN sounds like VAH-gen, close to wager: when you wager, you dare to risk something.

example.en: The devil is in the details.

cards.trick: TEUFEL sounds like "toy fell": the devil grins whenever a child's toy fell and broke.

cards.hint: one word: wo plus the word for of, from
cards.trick: WOVON (say voh-FON) is wo plus von glued together, like asking what-of or what-from in one word.

cards.hint: two-letter word, not jemals or schon mal

example.target: Das war besser als je zuvor.

cards.trick: JE sounds like yeah: have you ever said yeah to something crazy?

cards.hint: as in what kind of music

example.target: Welche Art von Musik magst du?
example.en: What kind of music do you like?

cards.trick: ART sounds like English art, and there are many kinds of art: painting, music, dance.

cards.en: call me [as soon as] you're home

example.target: Ruf mich an, sobald du zu Hause bist.
example.en: Call me as soon as you're home.

cards.trick: SOBALD is so plus bald, German for soon: picture a man who goes bald as soon as he hears the news.
SCHULD sounds like "should": you should have known better, so it's your fault.

cards.en: You can stay [as long as] you want.

example.target: Du kannst bleiben, solange du willst.
example.en: You can stay as long as you want.

cards.trick: SOLANGE sounds like zo-LANG-uh, close to "so long": stay so long, as long as you like.
MAMA sounds just like English mama, MAH-mah, the word kids everywhere use for their mom.
cards.why: Use Mama for the casual mom; die Mutter is the neutral word for mother.

example.target: Ich gehe raus, obwohl es regnet.
example.en: I'm going out, although it's raining.

cards.trick: OBWOHL sounds like 'op, vole!': although it's pouring, the little vole pops out anyway.
The middle of verTRAUen sounds a bit like true, and you trust people who stay true to you.
DAGEGEN is da (there) plus gegen, said GAY-gen, meaning against: there-against, so against that, against it.

example.target: Auf welcher Seite stehst du eigentlich?
example.en: Whose side are you on, anyway?

cards.trick: SEITE sounds like ZY-tuh, close to side: every coin has two sides.

cards.hint: some but not all, many a; not einige

example.target: Manche Leute verstehen das einfach nicht.
example.en: Some people just don't get it.

cards.trick: MANCH sounds like "munch": some days you munch a lot, some days you don't.
cards.why: Use manch for some but not others (many a); use einige for a small number, a few.

cards.hint: the noun, as in keep a promise

example.target: Du hast dein Versprechen nicht gehalten.

cards.trick: Das VERSPRECHEN sounds like fair-SHPREKH-en, holding sprechen (to speak): a promise is a word you speak and must keep.

cards.hint: not busy or captive, not free of charge
cards.trick: FREI sounds like "fry": the fish jumped out of the frying pan and was free.

cards.hint: a location, also a village (not Platz)
cards.trick: ORT rhymes with fort, and a fort is a place you can find on a map.
cards.why: Use Ort for a location or village; Platz for a seat, free space or town square.

cards.hint: win against a team or rival, as in we beat them 3 to 1; the everyday word, not besiegen

example.target: Wir haben sie drei zu eins geschlagen.
example.en: We beat them three to one.

cards.trick: SCHLAGEN sounds like slug it out: you slug it out with your rival and beat them.

example.target: Warum bist du heute so ernst?
example.en: Why are you so serious today?

cards.trick: ERNST sounds like earnest, and an earnest person is serious.

example.target: Geschichte war in der Schule mein Lieblingsfach.
example.en: History was my favourite subject at school.

cards.trick: GESCHICHTE sounds like the verb geschehen, to happen: history is everything that has happened.
HASSEN sounds like hassle: you hate the hassle.

cards.hint: where something is, not where to
cards.trick: OBEN sounds like "Oh, Ben!", what you shout up to Ben, who is upstairs.

example.target: Gestern war ich den ganzen Tag zu Hause.
example.en: Yesterday I was at home all day.

cards.trick: GESTERN sounds like guess turn: yesterday you had to guess whose turn it was.
erWARTEN hides warten, said VAR-ten, meaning to wait: when you expect something, you wait for it.

example.target: Der Bus fährt an uns vorbei.

cards.trick: VORBEI sounds like for bye: you wave bye as a friend goes past you.

cards.hint: at last, after a long wait
cards.trick: ENDLICH starts with END: when something comes to an end after a long wait, it's finally over.

cards.hint: before a number; not ungefähr, rund or circa
cards.trick: ETWA sounds like 'ate va': I ate about ten waffles, roughly, I didn't count exactly.

cards.hint: not the same, as in it's different now
cards.trick: ANDERS sounds like and others: the others are always different.
cards.why: Use anders for different(ly) on its own; andere means other, before a noun.

cards.hint: an opportunity; the look-alike word, not Gelegenheit
cards.trick: CHANCE is English chance said the French way, SHAHN-suh: an opportunity you get.
FOLGEN begins with the same sound as follow, so when you folgen someone, you follow them.

example.en: We're getting married in the summer.

cards.trick: HEIRATEN starts with HEI, said like high: newlyweds are on a high on the day they marry.
WAHRHEIT sounds like VAR-hite: the VAR video replay in football shows the truth about what really happened.

cards.hint: to request something, not ask a question

example.target: Ich bitte dich um einen Gefallen.
example.en: I'm asking you for a favor.

cards.trick: BITTEN sounds like bidden, and when you bid someone do something, you ask them. It's related to bitte, please.
cards.why: Use bitten to request something (um + thing); use fragen to ask a question.

example.en: He was here just a moment ago.

cards.trick: EBEN sounds like AY-ben, close to English even: even a moment ago, just now, he was here.
cards.why: Use eben for something that happened a moment ago; gerade for something happening right now.

example.target: Meine Oma wohnt auf dem Land.
example.en: My grandma lives in the countryside.

cards.trick: LAND sounds like English land with a t at the end: out in the countryside there is open land everywhere.

cards.hint: into a pocket or slot, not legen

example.target: Ich stecke das Handy in die Tasche.
example.en: I put my phone in my pocket.

cards.trick: STECKEN sounds like 'stick in': you stick your phone into your pocket.
cards.why: Use stecken for putting something into a pocket or slot; legen for laying it flat, stellen for standing it upright.

cards.trick: SPASS is said SHPAHSS, like spa with a sh at the front: a day at the spa is pure fun.
LÜGEN sounds a bit like lug in: a liar lugs in one fake story after another.
cards.why: Use lügen for telling an untruth; liegen is to lie down or be located.

cards.hint: in a home or hotel, not Raum
cards.trick: ZIMMER sounds like tsimmer, close to simmer: you sit and simmer quietly in your room.

example.target: Ich freue mich, dass du da bist.

cards.trick: FREUEN sounds like FROY-en, close to the name Freud, and Freude is the German word for joy.

example.target: Der Kuchen ist mir zu süß.
example.en: The cake is too sweet for me.

cards.trick: SÜSS sounds a bit like Seuss, and Dr. Seuss stories are as sweet as candy.

example.target: Mein Opa hat nie über den Krieg gesprochen.
example.en: My grandpa never talked about the war.

cards.trick: KRIEG sounds like creek: two armies at war on opposite banks of a creek.

cards.hint: to alter something, not swap it; the short everyday word, not verändern
cards.trick: ÄNDERN starts like the English word end: change a story by rewriting its end.
cards.why: Use ändern to alter or adjust something; verändern for a deeper change that makes it really different.

cards.trick: GEWINNEN sounds like geh-VIN-nen, and the middle is just English win said with a German v.
BETT sounds like English bed said with a hard t at the end, and it means a bed.

cards.hint: emphatic, the longer word, not nie
