cards.trick: NIEMALS sounds like knee malls: you will never find a mall built for knees.
cards.why: Use nie for an everyday never; niemals is the stronger, emphatic never.

example.target: Du bist stärker, als du denkst.

cards.trick: STARK sounds like Tony Stark, Iron Man, who is very strong in his suit.

example.target: Komm bitte so schnell wie möglich.
example.en: Please come as fast as possible.

cards.trick: MÖGLICH sounds a bit like "mug-lick": licking a mug totally clean? Sure, it's possible.
The end of geSICHT sounds a bit like sight: your face is the first sight people get of you.

example.target: Kannst du mir das noch mal erklären?
example.en: Can you explain that to me again?

cards.trick: ErKLÄREN sounds like air-CLAIR-en, with clear in the middle: to explain something is to make it clear.
MANCHMAL sounds like munch-mahl: sometimes I munch a meal. It is also manch (many a) plus mal (time): many a time.

example.target: Ich wünsche dir alles Gute zum Geburtstag!
example.en: I wish you a happy birthday!

cards.trick: WÜNSCHEN sounds a bit like "win-shen": when you wish on a star, you wish to win.
FLIEGEN sounds like flee again: a scared bird flees again by flying away.
VERKAUFEN sounds like fair COW-fen: at the fair, you sell your cow.
cards.why: Verkaufen is to sell; kaufen, without ver-, is to buy.

cards.hint: how someone does something, the short word that also means kind or sort; not Weise

example.target: Ich mag deine Art zu reden.
example.en: I like the way you talk.

cards.trick: ART sounds like English art: the art of doing something is your own way of doing it.
cards.why: Use Art for the way someone does something; der Weg is the way you travel, a route or path.

cards.trick: FREUNDIN sounds like FROYND-in, close to friend plus -in: the friend who is in your heart is your girlfriend.
cards.why: Meine Freundin usually means your girlfriend; for a female friend say eine Freundin.

cards.hint: money you owe; give the singular, though it's mostly used in the plural (Schulden)

example.target: Er hat viele Schulden bei der Bank.
example.en: He has a lot of debts with the bank.

cards.trick: SCHULD sounds like "should": a debt is money you should pay back.

example.target: Ich gehe morgen nicht in die Schule.
example.en: I'm not going to school tomorrow.

cards.trick: SCHULE sounds like SHOO-luh, which is just school with an extra syllable on the end.

regional.text: benützen is the usual form (also in Switzerland and southern Germany)

cards.trick: BeNUTZen hides NUTZ, which sounds a lot like nuts: a squirrel uses a stone to crack its nuts.

example.target: Ich habe ein gutes Gefühl dabei.
example.en: I have a good feeling about it.

cards.trick: geFÜHL sounds a lot like "feel": a feeling is what you feel.

example.target: Vertrauen ist in einer Beziehung sehr wichtig.
example.en: Trust is very important in a relationship.

cards.trick: Das verTRAUen has TRAU in the middle, which sounds a bit like true: trust is what you give someone who is true.
FEST sounds like fast in hold fast or stuck fast: something held fast is firm and tight.
SEITE sounds like ZY-tuh, a bit like site: a website is made of pages, and each page has two sides.
BEGINNEN sounds like begin with an extra -nen tacked on, and it means exactly that: to begin.
cards.why: Beginnen is a little more formal; in everyday talk anfangen is the usual word for start.

example.en: My brother earns really good money.

cards.trick: verDIENen sounds like fair dinin': you earn money so you can afford a fair bit of dining out.

example.target: Ich hoffe, wir sehen uns bald wieder.
example.en: I hope we see each other again soon.

cards.trick: WIEDERSEHEN sounds like VEE-der-ZAY-en: wieder means again, and sehen sounds a bit like see, so it means see again.

example.target: Sei ehrlich, gefällt dir mein Kleid?
example.en: Be honest, do you like my dress?

cards.trick: EHRLICH sounds like air-lick: an honest person is clear as air, with nothing hidden.
DAUERN, said DOW-ern, is related to duration and endure: how long something lasts.

example.target: Da ist Blut auf deinem Hemd.

cards.trick: BLUT sounds like bloot, almost the English word blood with a hard t at the end.

cards.hint: the everyday one word, not Entschuldige or Verzeihung, said to apologize or get a stranger's attention

example.target: Entschuldigung, wo ist hier der Bahnhof?
example.en: Excuse me, where's the train station?

cards.trick: ent-SHOOL-di-goong has SHOOL in the middle, like 'should': you say it when you should have been more careful.

example.en: I just wanted to ask quickly.

cards.trick: BLOSS sounds like blows: it was just one blow, only a little one.
AUF-HÖREN sounds like "off hearing": when you stop doing something, you switch off and stop hearing it.
cards.why: Use aufhören when you stop doing something; halten when a bus or car stops, aufhalten when you stop someone.

cards.trick: HUND sounds like hoont, close to hound, and a hound is a dog.
FUNKTIONIEREN sounds like "function": when something functions, it works.
cards.why: Use funktionieren when a machine or plan works; arbeiten when a person does work.

example.target: Ich schicke dir gleich eine Nachricht.
example.en: I'll send you a message in a minute.

cards.trick: NACHRICHT starts like "knock": a message knocks on your phone with a ping.

cards.hint: your spot, as in is this one free?

example.target: Ist der Platz hier noch frei?

cards.trick: PLATZ sounds like plots: at a wedding every guest gets a little plot, a seat of their own.
WEISS sounds like vice: picture the Miami Vice detectives in their famous white suits.
GESCHEHEN sounds like guh-SHAY-en: picture someone shaking, asking what on earth just happened.
cards.why: Geschehen is a bit formal; in everyday talk, passieren is the usual word for to happen.

example.target: Schließ bitte die Tür, es zieht.
example.en: Please close the door, there's a draft.

cards.trick: SCHLIESSEN sounds like "shh, Lisa": Shh, Lisa, close the door quietly.
HART sounds like heart: someone with a heart of stone is hard and tough.
cards.why: Use hart for firm, tough things; schwer for a hard task or something difficult.

example.target: Das ist der beste Teil vom Film.
example.en: That's the best part of the movie.

cards.trick: TEIL sounds like "tile": one tile is just a small part of the whole floor.

cards.hint: a battle or struggle, not an argument
cards.trick: KAMPF sounds like camp: soldiers march out of their camp to fight.

example.target: Die Musik ist mir zu laut.
example.en: The music is too loud for me.

cards.trick: LAUT sounds like "lout", and a lout is always loud.

example.target: Ich lese gerade ein spannendes Buch.
example.en: I'm reading an exciting book right now.

cards.trick: BUCH sounds like book said with a scratchy throat at the end, and it means book.

cards.hint: where something is, not where it moves to
cards.trick: UNTEN sounds a bit like "under": whatever is under you is below, downstairs.

cards.hint: no object, same verb as to put in, as in Wo ___ du? (Where are you?)
cards.trick: STECK-en sounds like 'stuck in': when you're stuck in traffic, you 'steckst' in traffic.

cards.hint: kidding, the same word as fun (not Scherz or Witz)

example.target: Keine Angst, das war nur Spaß!
example.en: Don't worry, it was just a joke!

cards.trick: SPASS sounds like shpass: just kidding, so let it pass, it was only a joke.
cards.why: Use Spaß for kidding around (nur Spaß); Witz for a joke you tell.

example.target: Das Schiff fährt um acht Uhr ab.
example.en: The ship leaves at eight o'clock.

cards.trick: SCHIFF sounds like "ship" with an f at the end: a big ship sailing off.

example.target: Wollen wir heute Abend einen Film schauen?
example.en: Shall we watch a movie tonight?

cards.trick: FILM sounds just like the English word film, and a film is a movie.

example.target: Ich freue mich auf das Wochenende.
example.en: I'm looking forward to the weekend.

cards.trick: FREUEN sounds like FROY-en, like Freud, and Freude means joy: you feel joy now about what's coming.
cards.why: With auf it means looking forward to something ahead; without auf it is being glad about now.

regional.text: Swiss speakers commonly say herzig (härzig) for cute, as in Dä Hund isch so härzig!

cards.trick: SÜSS starts with a z sound, a bit like zoos, where the baby animals are so cute.

cards.hint: not hard; the word that also means light in weight
cards.trick: LEICHT sounds almost like light: a light job is an easy job.
SCHIESSEN starts with a sh sound, SHEE-sen, like the start of shoot, and its past schoss sounds close to shot.

example.target: Wie oft gehst du ins Kino?
example.en: How often do you go to the cinema?

cards.trick: OFT sounds like the old English word oft, as in an oft-told story: something that happens often.

example.target: Mein Computer ist heute total langsam.
example.en: My computer is really slow today.

cards.trick: LANGSAM sounds like "long-zahm", like "long, some": slow things take a long time.

cards.hint: the look-alike word, not blöd or doof
cards.trick: DUMM sounds almost exactly like English dumb, and it means just that: stupid.

example.en: Why are you shouting like that?

cards.trick: SCHREIEN sounds like "shry-en", and SCHREI rhymes with "cry": you cry out when you scream.
ELTERN sounds like "elders": your parents are your elders.

cards.hint: a phone or room number, not a quantity
cards.trick: NUMMER, said NOOM-er, sounds like number with the b swallowed: give me your number.

example.target: Du wirfst den Ball zu weit.
example.en: You're throwing the ball too far.

cards.trick: WERFEN starts like VAIRF, close to verve: you throw a ball with verve.

example.target: Mein Papa holt mich heute ab.
example.en: My dad is picking me up today.

cards.trick: PAPA sounds just like the English papa, the word kids use for their dad.

example.en: Who does this phone belong to?

cards.trick: geHÖRen sounds a bit like guh-HER-en: whose bag is this? It belongs to HER.

cards.hint: appearance, as in to look tired

example.target: Du siehst heute echt müde aus.

cards.trick: AUS-SEHEN is aus (out, said like OWSS) plus sehen (to see, said ZAY-en): what others see from the outside is how you look.

cards.hint: at the end, as in um den See ...; not um alone

example.target: Wir laufen um den See herum.

cards.trick: HERUM sounds like "hair room": your hair needs room all around your head.
IRgend-VEE: wie, said vee, means how, and irgend means some, so irgendwie is literally some-how.

example.target: Das ist Lena, eine Freundin aus der Schule.
example.en: This is Lena, a friend from school.

cards.trick: FREUNDIN sounds like FROYND-in: Freund sounds like friend, and the ending -in marks a woman.
cards.why: Say eine Freundin (von mir) for a female friend; meine Freundin often sounds like girlfriend.

example.target: Der König lebt in einem großen Schloss.
example.en: The king lives in a big castle.

cards.trick: KÖNIG is a cousin of the English word king: both start with K-, and the KÖ-nig wears the crown.

example.target: Komm, ich führe dich durch die Altstadt.
example.en: Come on, I'll show you around the old town.

cards.trick: FÜHREN sounds a bit like fur-en: picture a guide in a fur coat leading the group through the snow.
KAUM sounds like cow plus m: a cow can hardly climb the stairs.
NAH sounds like "naa", English "near" said with the r dropped: something nah is near.

example.en: How did you find out about that?

cards.trick: ERFAHREN sounds like "air far-en": news travels far through the air until you find it out.

cards.hint: the general word, not specifically a mobile
cards.trick: TELEFON sounds like telephone with the stress on the end, tay-lay-FOHN, and it means phone.

example.target: Du solltest morgen zum Arzt gehen.
example.en: You should go to the doctor tomorrow.

cards.trick: ARZT sounds like "arts": a doctor practises the healing arts.
cards.why: Use Arzt for the doctor you go to see; Doktor is mostly the title (Herr Doktor).

example.target: Kannst du bitte das Fenster öffnen?
example.en: Can you open the window, please?

cards.trick: ÖFFNEN sounds a bit like oven: you open the oven door to check the cake.
verDIENen sounds like fair dinner: after all that work, you deserve a fair dinner.

example.target: Auf Wiedersehen, und danke für alles!

cards.trick: AUF WIEDERSEHEN sounds like owf VEE-der-ZAY-en, literally until we see again, which is a polite goodbye.

example.target: Wir machen heute Abend ein Feuer im Garten.
example.en: We're making a fire in the garden tonight.

cards.trick: FEUER sounds like foyer: picture a big fire crackling in a hotel foyer.

cards.hint: sooner than planned, the comparative of early
cards.trick: FRÜH-er sounds a bit like free-er: if you finish earlier, you're free-er sooner.

example.target: Keine Sorge, ich erledige das morgen.
example.en: Don't worry, I'll take care of it tomorrow.

cards.trick: ERLEDIGEN sounds like air-LAY-dig-en: air out the room, lay the table, dig the garden, and your jobs are taken care of.
cards.why: Use erledigen for getting a task done; sich kümmern um for looking after someone or something.

example.target: Ich warte noch auf deine Entschuldigung.
example.en: I'm still waiting for your apology.

cards.trick: ent-SHOOL-di-goong hides SHOOL, like 'should': an apology admits what you should have done differently.

cards.hint: as in with bare hands, not nackt

example.target: Er hat den Fisch mit bloßen Händen gefangen.
example.en: He caught the fish with his bare hands.

cards.trick: BLOSS sounds like blows: the cold wind blows on your bare hands.

cards.hint: someone or yourself, not it hurts
cards.trick: VERLETZEN sounds like fair-LETS-en: it's not fair to let someone get hurt.
cards.why: Use verletzen for injuring someone or yourself; use wehtun when something hurts.

example.target: Du siehst heute echt hübsch aus.

cards.trick: HÜBSCH sounds a bit like hub-sh: the prettiest face at the party hub makes everyone go shh and stare.
cards.why: Use hübsch for pretty, good-looking people or things; schön is the broader word for beautiful or nice.

cards.hint: before anything else, as in first we eat, then...; not erst, erstens or zunächst

example.target: Zuerst essen wir, dann gehen wir ins Kino.
example.en: First we'll eat, then we'll go to the cinema.

cards.trick: ZUERST sounds like tsoo-AIRST, almost to first: whatever you do zuerst, you do first.
cards.why: Use zuerst for doing something first, before anything else; erste is the adjective, as in der erste Tag.

cards.hint: a piece of news; plural for the TV news

example.target: Ich habe eine gute Nachricht für dich!
example.en: I have good news for you!

cards.trick: NACHRICHTEN sounds like "knock-rikh-ten": the evening news knocks at ten, right on time.

cards.hint: free space, as in no room left

example.target: Wir haben keinen Platz mehr im Auto.
example.en: We have no room left in the car.

cards.trick: PLATZ sounds like plots: an empty plot of land means there is still room to build.
WAHRSCHEINLICH sounds like var-SHINE-likh: the sun will probably shine tomorrow.
cards.why: Wahrscheinlich is the full, clear word for probably; wohl is the short, vaguer one, often a guess.

example.en: That doesn't interest me at all.

cards.trick: INTERESSIEREN starts with the sound of interest, plus the -ieren ending German puts on borrowed verbs: to interest.
STRASSE, said "SHTRAH-suh", and English "street" both come from the Latin word for a paved road, strata.

example.target: Ich bin froh, dass du da bist.

cards.trick: FROH rhymes with "go": you're so glad about the news that you shout "Go, go, go!"
cards.why: Use froh for being glad or relieved about something; glücklich for being truly happy.

cards.trick: FEHLER sounds like failure: a failure usually comes from a mistake.
DOLLAR sounds almost exactly like English dollar, with the stress on DOL, and it means the same money.

cards.hint: polite word, as in ladies and gentlemen

example.target: Die Dame da drüben wartet auf dich.
example.en: The lady over there is waiting for you.

cards.trick: DAME sounds like DAH-muh, close to the English title Dame, given to an honoured lady.
WILLKOMMEN sounds like "vill come in": when guests will come in, you tell them they're welcome.

example.en: What are you planning for the weekend?

cards.trick: PLANEN sounds like "plan-en": you just add -en to plan, and you get to plan.

example.target: Wir haben heute eine Menge Arbeit.
example.en: We have a lot of work today.

cards.trick: MENGE starts like many: many things make a big amount.

cards.hint: to this place, with motion; the long word built on hier, not her
cards.trick: HIERHER sounds like "here-hair": it is hier (here) plus her (toward me), so it means coming here.
cards.why: Use hierher when someone or something moves to here; use hier for where something is.

cards.trick: BÜRO sounds like "bureau", as in FBI bureau: a bureau is an office.

example.target: Ich hatte heute Nacht einen komischen Traum.
example.en: I had a weird dream last night.

cards.trick: TRAUM sounds like a short TROW-m, almost trauma: a bad dream can feel like a little trauma.

example.target: Ich stelle dir meine Schwester vor.
example.en: I'll introduce my sister to you.

cards.trick: VOR-shtellen sounds like fore-tell: you put someone to the fore and tell everyone their name.

example.target: Ich komme direkt nach der Arbeit.

cards.trick: DIREKT sounds like dee-REKT, almost the English word direct, and it means the same thing.
LEICHT sounds almost like light, and it means exactly that: not heavy.

cards.hint: a plan going well, informal, not funktionieren
cards.trick: KLAPPEN sounds like clapping: when your plan works out, everyone claps.

cards.hint: a bone, a promise, a rule

example.target: Ich habe mir das Bein gebrochen.

cards.trick: BRECHEN sounds like a throaty "break-en": to break something.

example.target: Ich bin in zehn Minuten da.
example.en: I'll be there in ten minutes.

cards.trick: ZEHN (say tsayn) rhymes with rain: it rained for ten days straight.

example.target: Ich reise im Sommer nach Italien.
example.en: I'm traveling to Italy in the summer.

cards.trick: REISEN sounds like rising: you rise early on the day you travel.

example.target: Das Spiel fängt um acht an.

cards.trick: SPIEL sounds like shpeel, like the English spiel: every new game starts with a long spiel explaining the rules.
SINGEN, said ZING-en, is just English sing with a buzzy z sound and -en on the end.

example.target: Schau mal, das Bild hat meine Oma gemalt.
example.en: Look, my grandma painted this picture.

cards.trick: BILD sounds like "built": a painter builds a picture stroke by stroke.
PERFEKT sounds almost exactly like perfect, just with the stress on the end: per-FEKT.
BeSHTIMMT has stimmt inside it, German for that's right, so if it's bestimmt, it's definitely right.

cards.hint: a bit more formal, not schon
cards.trick: BEREITS (buh-RITES) holds bereit, meaning ready: when everything is all ready, it is already done.
cards.why: Bereits means the same as schon but sounds more formal; in everyday speech use schon.

example.target: Ich stehe jeden Tag um sechs auf.
example.en: I get up at six every day.

cards.trick: SECHS sounds like "zeks", which is just English "six" said with a buzzing z at the start.

example.target: Ich lade gerade die Kisten ins Auto.
example.en: I'm loading the boxes into the car right now.

cards.trick: LADEN is the English word laden: a truck laden with boxes is one somebody has loaded.
SCHWARZ sounds like "shvarts", close to "swarthy", which means dark, and black is the darkest colour.

example.en: My dad is building a garage.

cards.trick: BAUEN sounds like "bower", the shelter a bowerbird builds for itself.

example.target: Das war kein Unfall, das war Mord.
example.en: That wasn't an accident, that was murder.

cards.trick: MORD sounds like mort, as in mortuary: a murder sends someone to the mortuary.
SEKUNDE, said zeh-KOON-duh, is just English second with a German ending: sixty of them make a minute.
RATEN sounds like rotten: guess which of these apples is rotten.

cards.hint: magnificent; the long word built from 'big', not toll or super
cards.trick: GROSSARTIG sounds like grand art-ish: something grand like a work of art is great.
ERFAHREN hides fahren, to travel: someone who has travelled far is experienced.

cards.hint: deals, commerce, as in business is going well; not a company

example.target: Das Geschäft läuft gerade richtig gut.
example.en: Business is going really well right now.

cards.trick: GeSCHÄFT ends like "shaft": in a bad business deal you get the shaft.

example.target: Dein neues Fahrrad ist echt cool.
example.en: Your new bike is really cool.

cards.trick: COOL is borrowed straight from English and sounds the same; Germans use it for awesome or laid-back, but never for chilly.

example.target: Ich habe heute leider keine Zeit.
example.en: Unfortunately, I don't have time today.

cards.trick: LEIDER sounds a bit like lighter: unfortunately, my lighter won't work.
erKENNen has KEN in it: when someone comes back within your ken, you recognize them.
OPFER sounds like "offer": the victim was offered up to the villain.

example.target: Was ist dein Plan für heute?

cards.trick: PLAN sounds almost like the English plan, just with a long ah: plahn. Same word, same meaning.

cards.hint: in former times, as in I used to live there

example.target: Früher habe ich in Berlin gewohnt.
example.en: I used to live in Berlin.

cards.trick: FRÜH-er sounds like free-er: in the past, before all the responsibilities, you were free-er.

example.target: Das alte Auto ist nicht viel wert.
example.en: The old car isn't worth much.

cards.trick: WERT sounds like vairt, a close cousin of English worth: what is it worth?
FOTO sounds just like photo, and that's exactly what it means: a picture you take with a camera.

example.target: Er hat eine Million Euro gewonnen.

cards.trick: MILLION sounds like English million said with a French flair, mil-YOHN, and it means the same thing.

example.target: Willst du noch ein Stück Kuchen?
example.en: Do you want another piece of cake?

cards.trick: STÜCK sounds a bit like "stuck": a piece of cake got stuck in your throat.

example.target: Die Woche war echt die Hölle.

cards.trick: HÖLLE sounds a lot like hell with an extra uh on the end, and it means just that: hell.

cards.hint: also the title, as in Herr Doktor; not Arzt

example.target: Danke, Herr Doktor, mir geht's schon besser.
example.en: Thanks, doctor, I'm already feeling better.

cards.trick: DOKTOR is spelled with a k but sounds almost exactly like English doctor.
cards.why: Use Doktor as a title or when addressing one (Herr Doktor); Arzt is the usual word for the doctor you go to.

cards.trick: WEINEN sounds like VINE-en, close to English whine: a child who whines soon starts to cry.

cards.hint: an open area in a town

example.target: Wir treffen uns auf dem Platz vor der Kirche.
example.en: Let's meet in the square in front of the church.

cards.trick: PLATZ sounds a bit like plaza, and a plaza is a town square.
TANZ sounds like TANTS, almost the English word dance said with a T at the front.

example.target: Ich sehe mir das Foto an.

cards.trick: ANSEHEN sounds like "on ZAY-en": you set your eyes on something and see it, so you look at it.

example.target: Es regnet, aber wir gehen trotzdem raus.
example.en: It's raining, but we're going out anyway.

cards.trick: TROTZDEM sounds like trots them: the horse trots on anyway, despite them.
KUMPEL sounds like KOOM-pel, close to come, pal! That's what you say to your buddy.

cards.hint: casual, as in totally tired; the look-alike word, not voll, völlig or komplett
cards.trick: TOTAL sounds like English total with the stress at the end, toh-TAHL: something total is totally done.

cards.hint: related to voll (full), the short word, not ganz or vollkommen
cards.trick: VÖLLIG sounds a bit like "full-ish": something filled full is completely full.
FEHLEN sounds like "FAIL-en": something that fails to turn up is missing.

cards.hint: before a noun, as in half an hour, not die Hälfte

example.target: Ich warte schon eine halbe Stunde auf dich.
example.en: I've been waiting for you for half an hour.

cards.trick: HALB is said like halp, which sounds almost like half.

example.target: Dein Bild hängt jetzt an der Wand.
example.en: Your picture is hanging on the wall now.

cards.trick: HÄNGEN sounds almost like "hang-en": you hang a picture, and it hangs on the wall.

cards.hint: a crowd of people; the short word, not Menschenmenge

example.target: Ich habe dich in der Menge verloren.
example.en: I lost you in the crowd.

cards.trick: MENGE sounds a bit like mingle: people mingle in a crowd.
ÜBERALL sounds like over all: something spread over all places is everywhere.

example.target: Der Himmel ist heute so blau.
example.en: The sky is so blue today.

cards.trick: HIMMEL sounds like "hymn-all": birds sing a hymn all across the sky.

example.target: Keine Sorge, das ist ganz normal.

cards.trick: NORMAL is just English normal, said nor-MAHL with the stress at the end.

cards.hint: picture it in your mind, with sich

example.target: Stell dir vor, Anna ist schwanger!

cards.trick: VOR-shtellen sounds like fore-stall: you stall a picture in the fore of your mind, right in front of your mind's eye.
cards.why: Add mir or dir (Ich stelle mir vor) to mean imagine; without it, vorstellen means to introduce someone.

cards.hint: hold on to, not give back
cards.trick: BeHALTen has halten in it, which sounds like "hold": to keep is to hold on to something.
STEHLEN sounds like "shtay-len", close to "stealing": to stehlen is to steal.

cards.hint: the noun, as in turn on the light
cards.trick: LICHT sounds almost like "light", just with a soft breathy ch sound where English has the gh.

example.target: Wir essen zuerst, danach gehen wir ins Kino.
example.en: We'll eat first, and after that we'll go to the cinema.

cards.trick: DANACH sounds like "the knock": first dinner, and after that comes the knock at the door.

example.target: Das ist schon mein zweiter Kaffee heute.
example.en: That's already my second coffee today.

cards.trick: ZWEITE is ZWEI (said tsvai, two) plus -te, like saying two-th: the second one in line.
LUFT sounds like aloft: something aloft is up in the air.

example.target: Ich warte noch auf deine Antwort.
example.en: I'm still waiting for your answer.

cards.trick: ANTWORT sounds like ant-vort, an ant word: the ant gave a one-word answer.

cards.hint: pass on an incident such as an accident or a problem to the police or a boss (not anzeigen or berichten)

example.target: Wir haben den Unfall der Polizei gemeldet.
example.en: We reported the accident to the police.

cards.trick: MELDEN sounds like "mailed in": when you report something, you've mailed it in to the people in charge.

example.target: Der See ist hier sehr tief.
example.en: The lake is very deep here.

cards.trick: TIEF sounds like teef, close to thief: a thief hides his loot deep underground.

cards.hint: get hold of something, often by buying it, for someone; not holen (fetch) or bekommen

example.target: Ich besorge dir morgen ein Ticket.
example.en: I'll get you a ticket tomorrow.

cards.trick: BESORGEN sounds like be-ZOR-gen: picture an alien called Zorg who runs off to get you whatever you need.
cards.why: Use besorgen when you go and get something for someone; bekommen when you receive it.

example.en: Are you looking for a certain book?

cards.trick: BeSHTIMMT sounds like be-stamped: a thing someone has stamped and picked out is one certain, particular thing.

cards.hint: one individual, as in per person (not Mensch)

example.target: Wir brauchen einen Tisch für vier Personen.
example.en: We need a table for four people.

cards.trick: PERSON sounds like "pair-ZOHN": it is the English word person, just said with a z sound and the stress at the end.
cards.why: Use Person for one individual you count (für vier Personen); Mensch for a human being in general.

cards.trick: entSCHEIDen sounds like ent-SHY-den: a shy Ent hiding in his den has to decide whether to come out.
cards.why: Use entscheiden for making a choice; bestimmen when you are the one in charge who decides.

example.target: Der Sturm hat das Dach zerstört.

cards.trick: ZERSTÖREN sounds like "tsar stirring": an angry tsar stirring up a war destroys whole cities.

cards.hint: meaning, as in it makes sense
cards.trick: SINN, said like zin, sounds like a short sense: when something has Sinn, it makes sense.

example.target: Die Erde dreht sich um die Sonne.
example.en: The Earth goes around the sun.

cards.trick: ERDE sounds like a German way of saying earth, with a d where English has th: our planet Earth.
BEWEISEN sounds like be-VYE-zen, close to be wise: be wise and prove what you claim.

cards.hint: related to der Schreck, a fright
cards.trick: SCHRECK-lich sounds like Shrek: the villagers think the ogre Shrek looks terrible and awful.

cards.hint: tell someone what you think they should do, as in I ___ you to stay; not beraten or empfehlen

example.target: Ich rate dir, heute zu Hause zu bleiben.
example.en: I advise you to stay home today.

cards.trick: RATEN sounds like rotten: I advise you not to eat that rotten fish.

cards.hint: a criminal, said of the police; not fangen, schnappen or festnehmen

example.target: Die Polizei hat den Dieb gestern gefasst.
example.en: The police caught the thief yesterday.

cards.trick: FASSEN sounds like "fasten": the police fasten handcuffs on the thief they catch.

example.en: Turn the key to the left.

cards.trick: DREHEN sounds like "DRAY-en", close to "drain": water turns round and round as it goes down the drain.

cards.hint: the word that also means business

example.target: Das Geschäft macht um acht zu.

cards.trick: GeSCHÄFT sounds a bit like "shelfed": a store is full of shelfed goods.
BEWEGEN sounds like "buh-VAY-gun" and hides Weg, German for way: move out of the way!

cards.hint: be painful; the everyday word, not schmerzen
cards.trick: WEH sounds like the vey in oy vey, which is what you groan when something hurts.

cards.hint: as in I have no choice
cards.trick: WAHL sounds like vahl, close to value: when you have a choice, you pick what you value most.

example.target: Für meine Kinder bringe ich jedes Opfer.
example.en: I'd make any sacrifice for my kids.

cards.trick: OPFER sounds like "offer": a sacrifice is something you offer up to the gods.
Onkel sounds almost exactly like uncle with an o at the front: your Onkel is your uncle.

example.target: Pass auf, die Straße ist gefährlich.
example.en: Watch out, the road is dangerous.

cards.trick: GefÄHRlich sounds like geh-FAIR-likh: the wild rides at the FAIR look dangerous.

cards.hint: a funny story you tell, not Scherz or Spaß
cards.trick: WITZ sounds like vits, close to wits: it takes quick wits to tell a good joke.
cards.why: Use Witz for a joke you tell; Spaß is fun or kidding around.

cards.trick: KOMISCH sounds like comic-ish: comic situations are often just plain weird.
FUSS sounds like "fooss", almost "foot": the man made a fuss about his sore foot.

cards.hint: in a theater; the short word, not Theaterstück
cards.trick: STÜCK sounds a bit like "stuck": the actor forgot his lines and got stuck in the middle of the play.

cards.hint: makes you laugh; the everyday word, not witzig
cards.trick: LUSTIG sounds like LOOSE-tickle: a loose tickle makes you laugh, so it's funny.

example.target: Kannst du morgen meine Schicht übernehmen?
example.en: Can you take over my shift tomorrow?

cards.trick: ÜBER sounds like over and NEHMEN (NAY-men) means to take, so übernehmen is literally to take over.

cards.hint: casual, also annoying; not dumm or doof

example.target: Das war echt eine blöde Idee.
example.en: That was a really dumb idea.

cards.trick: BLÖD sounds a bit like blurt: blurting things out without thinking is dumb.
cards.why: Use blöd for casual 'dumb' or 'annoying'; dumm is the plain word for stupid.

cards.hint: awesome, the word English also has; not toll
cards.trick: SUPER, said like ZOO-per, is just English super: something super is great.

cards.hint: a place, a train, someone by phone

example.target: Ich erreiche ihn nicht, sein Handy ist aus.
example.en: I can't reach him, his phone is off.

cards.trick: The middle of erREICHen sounds like reach said with an eye sound: you reach the station just in time.
BefEHL sounds like be-FAIL: if you ignore an order from the general, you're going to fail.

example.en: There's a dead body in the forest.

cards.trick: LEICHE starts with the sound of lie, like LYE-heh: a corpse just lies there and never gets up.
KOSTEN sounds like "costing": what is it costing you?
KÖRPER sounds a bit like corpse, and a corpse is a dead body.
WUNDERBAR sounds like VOON-der-bar, close to wonder bar: a place full of wonder is wonderful.

cards.hint: at that time in the past, not früher

example.target: Damals war ich noch ein Kind.
example.en: Back then I was still a kid.

cards.trick: DAMALS sounds like "the malls": back then, everyone hung out at the malls.
cards.why: Use damals for one particular time back then; früher for how things used to be in general.

example.target: Er hat mich ans Bein getreten.
example.en: He kicked me in the leg.

cards.trick: TREH-ten sounds like tread on: tread on someone hard with your foot and that is a kick.
cards.why: Kicking someone or something takes haben in the Perfekt: er hat mich getreten.

cards.trick: EHRE sounds like "air-uh": a knight carries himself with an air of honor.

example.en: Am I bothering you right now?

cards.trick: STÖREN sounds like shtur-en, close to stir: someone who stirs things up while you work bothers you.
HAAR sounds almost exactly like English hair, and that is what it means.
HIMMEL starts with the sound of "hymn": angels sing hymns in heaven.
PERSÖNLICH starts with the German word Person, and it sounds a lot like personal: it's all about one person.
UN-GLAUB-lich is built like un-believe-able: GLAUB, said GLOWP, comes from glauben, to believe.

cards.hint: be the one in charge, not entscheiden

example.en: I'm the one who decides here, not you.

cards.trick: BESTIMMEN hides Stimme, German for voice: whoever has the voice gets to decide.
cards.why: Use bestimmen when you're the one in charge who decides; entscheiden for making up your mind between choices.

cards.trick: REST sounds just like English rest, as in the rest of the cake: whatever is left over.

cards.hint: where something is, not where to

example.en: My keys are around here somewhere.

cards.trick: WO (said 'voh') means where, and IRGEND (EER-gent) means some or any, so irgendwo is somewhere.

example.en: I see it exactly the same way.

cards.trick: GENAUSO sounds like ge-NOW-zo: it is genau (exactly) plus so, so exactly so means just the same.

example.target: Niemand weiß, was die Zukunft bringt.
example.en: Nobody knows what the future will bring.

cards.trick: ZUKUNFT sounds like "tsoo-koonft", close to zukommen, "to come toward": the future is what is coming toward you.
ZAHLEN (TSAH-len) sounds a bit like tally: you tally up the bill, then you pay.
cards.why: Both mean pay; zahlen is the short everyday word, bezahlen is used with what you pay for (die Rechnung bezahlen).

example.target: Er sitzt seit zwei Jahren im Gefängnis.
example.en: He's been in prison for two years.

cards.trick: GeFÄNGnis sounds like "guh-FENG-niss", close to fang: a prison holds you in its fangs and won't let go.

example.target: Melde dich, wenn du angekommen bist!
example.en: Get in touch when you've arrived!

cards.trick: SICH MELDEN sounds like "meld in": you meld back into someone's day when you get in touch.
PFERD sounds like "fair-t": picture a horse winning first prize at the county fair.
BESORGT sounds like be-ZORKT, close to be sorrowed: worried people look full of sorrow.
KRAFT sounds like craft: any real craft, like building a boat by hand, takes strength and power.

example.target: Er hat den Mann einfach erschossen.
example.en: He just shot the man dead.

cards.trick: Inside erSCHIESSEN is schießen, said SHEE-sen, which begins like shoot; the er- in front makes it shoot dead.

cards.hint: across, on the other side; not dort

example.target: Dein Handy liegt da drüben auf dem Tisch.
example.en: Your phone is over there on the table.

cards.trick: DRÜBEN sounds a bit like DREW-ben: Ben drew a picture over there.
SCHLÜSSEL sounds a bit like shoe-sell: a shoe seller locks up his shop with a key every night.

example.target: Ich stehe morgen um acht auf.
example.en: I'm getting up at eight tomorrow.

cards.trick: ACHT, with its throaty ch, sounds a bit like the start of octopus, and an octopus has eight arms.

cards.hint: dirt in a garden or pot

example.en: Your hands are covered in soil.

cards.trick: ERDE is earth with a d: the brown earth you dig in the garden is soil.

example.target: Ich bin so stolz auf dich.

cards.trick: STOLZ, said 'shtolts', rhymes with 'bolts': a proud person stands bolt upright, chest out.

cards.hint: odd, not komisch, merkwürdig or eigenartig
cards.trick: SELTSAM, said ZELT-zahm, sounds a bit like seldom: something you seldom see seems strange.
cards.why: Seltsam is a little more careful or written; in casual talk Germans often say komisch for strange.

cards.trick: BEIN rhymes with fine and is a cousin of bone: your leg holds the longest bone in your body.

cards.hint: to take in, believe; as in I can't believe it

example.target: Ich kann es echt nicht fassen!

cards.trick: FASSEN sounds like "fasten": your mind can't fasten onto news too wild to grasp.

example.target: Wir drehen morgen eine Szene in Berlin.
example.en: We're shooting a scene in Berlin tomorrow.

cards.trick: DREHEN sounds like "DRAY-en": old film cameras had a crank you turned to shoot a film.
TEILEN sounds like "TILE-en": you cut a cake into tiles so everyone can share it.

example.target: Die Ampel ist rot, warte mal!

cards.trick: ROT sounds like "wrote": the teacher wrote all over your test in red ink.

example.target: Er arbeitet als Agent beim Geheimdienst.
example.en: He works as an agent for the secret service.

cards.trick: AGENT is the English word agent, but German says it ah-GENT with a hard g, like a secret agent whispering his code name.

example.en: Who's going to win the election?

cards.trick: WAHL sounds like vahl, a bit like ballot: in an election everyone drops a ballot in the box.

cards.hint: also still, as in be quiet!

example.target: Sei bitte still, das Baby schläft.
example.en: Please be quiet, the baby is sleeping.

cards.trick: STILL sounds like "shtill", close to English still: a still, silent room makes no sound at all.

cards.hint: more like, more likely (not lieber or ziemlich)

example.target: Er ist nicht dumm, eher faul.
example.en: He's not stupid, more like lazy.

cards.trick: EHER sounds a bit like AIR-uh: it's not really a cloud, it's rather just air.
cards.why: Use eher for more like or more likely; use lieber for what you'd prefer to do.

cards.trick: VERRATEN sounds a bit like fair rotten: betraying a friend is far from fair and truly rotten.
TEAM is borrowed from English and sounds just like it: a team is a team, but in German it takes das.

cards.hint: to reflect, ponder (separable verb, used with über)
cards.trick: DENKEN sounds like thinkin', and NACH sounds like knock: knock on your head while you keep thinkin' it over.

example.target: Sei vorsichtig, die Straße ist glatt.
example.en: Be careful, the road is slippery.

cards.trick: VORSICHTIG starts like FOR-ZIKH, close to "for sick": be careful when you're with someone sick.

example.target: Mein kleiner Bruder haut mich immer.
example.en: My little brother always hits me.

cards.trick: HAUEN starts with a sound like how, which rhymes with pow and ow: what you hear when someone hits you.
cards.why: Use hauen in casual talk; schlagen is the standard word for hitting.

cards.trick: FÜRCHTEN is a cousin of English fright, and to fear something is to feel fright.

cards.hint: mild everyday word, also shouted as Damn!

example.target: So ein Mist! Ich habe den Bus verpasst.
example.en: Damn it! I missed the bus.

cards.trick: MIST sounds just like English mist, but think of someone stepping in crap in the fog and yelling Mist!
ÄRGERN sounds a bit like argue-n: annoy people and they start to argue.

example.target: Der Supermarkt ist bis zehn Uhr offen.
example.en: The supermarket is open until ten.

cards.trick: OFFEN sounds like OFF-en: when the lid is off, the box is open.
cards.why: Offen is the standard adjective for open; auf is the short casual word, as in Die Tür ist auf.

cards.trick: ErREICHen holds reach: to achieve a goal is to finally reach it.
cards.why: Use erreichen for reaching a goal or result; schaffen for managing to get something done.

cards.hint: a group of students at school
cards.trick: KLASSE sounds like class with an extra uh on the end, and it means a school class.

example.target: Der Wolf im Märchen ist böse.
example.en: The wolf in the fairy tale is evil.

cards.trick: BÖSE sounds a little like bossy: the evil queen is the bossiest boss of all.

cards.hint: the short everyday word, not notwendig

example.target: Danke, aber das ist echt nicht nötig.
example.en: Thanks, but that's really not necessary.

cards.trick: NÖTIG sounds a bit like NEED-ish: what you need is necessary.
GEIST sounds like ghost with eye in the middle: a ghost floating through the house.
NOCHMAL sounds a bit like notch more: go one notch more and do it once again.
cards.why: Use nochmal for doing something one more time; wieder for again in general, like something happening once more.

cards.hint: the act, not male or female

example.target: In dem Film gibt es zu viel Sex.
example.en: There's too much sex in that film.

cards.trick: SEX is borrowed straight from English and means the same thing; just remember it takes der.

example.target: Sorry, ich bin dir auf den Fuß getreten.
example.en: Sorry, I stepped on your foot.

cards.trick: TREH-ten sounds like tread, and to tread is to step.
cards.why: Stepping on or into something takes sein in the Perfekt: ich bin getreten; kicking takes haben.

cards.trick: WOHNUNG sounds like VOH-noong, a bit like own nook: your own little nook in the city is your apartment.
BeRUHIGen hides ruhig, said ROO-ikh, meaning calm: picture a roo, a kangaroo, lying calm and still.

example.target: Beeil dich, der Zug fährt gleich!
example.en: Hurry up, the train's about to leave!

cards.trick: BEEILEN sounds like buh-EYE-len, as in buh, I'll be late, which is what you mutter as you hurry.

example.en: My grandpa is in the hospital.

cards.trick: KRANKENHAUS: krank sounds like cranky and Haus like house, so it's a house full of cranky sick people.

cards.hint: to realize, sense; the short word, not bemerken
cards.trick: MERKEN sounds like a mark: you notice something when it leaves a mark on your attention.

example.target: Ich habe keine Zeit. Außerdem bin ich müde.
example.en: I don't have time. Besides, I'm tired.

cards.trick: AUSSERDEM sounds like "OW, sir, DAME": the grumpy dame always has one more complaint besides.

cards.hint: almost certainly, I bet; not sicher or sicherlich
cards.trick: BESTIMMT hides Stimme, German for voice: say it in a firm voice and it means definitely.
cards.why: Use bestimmt for a confident guess (surely, I bet); sicher when you are certain or something is safe.

example.target: Willst du mit uns Karten spielen?
example.en: Do you want to play cards with us?

cards.trick: KARTE sounds like card with a little uh on the end: KAR-tuh, so just picture a card.
GEDANKE comes from denken, to think, and hides DANKE inside it: a thankful thought is still a thought.

cards.hint: as a consolation, not with numbers; built on wenig, not zumindest or immerhin

example.target: Es regnet, aber wenigstens ist es warm.
example.en: It's raining, but at least it's warm.

cards.trick: WENIGSTENS starts with wenig, said VAY-nikh, meaning a little: even a little is at least something.

example.target: Die Polizei hat den Mörder gefunden.

cards.trick: MÖRDER sounds almost like murder: a Mörder is the one who commits the murder.

example.target: Zum Glück haben alle den Unfall überlebt.

cards.trick: ÜBER-LEBEN: über is like over, and LEBEN sounds a bit like living, so you live on over danger: you survive.

example.target: Deine Jacke liegt auf dem Boden.
example.en: Your jacket is lying on the floor.

cards.trick: BODEN sounds a bit like bottom: the floor is the bottom of every room.
MUND sounds like "moont", close to "mouth": open your mouth wide like a round moon.

example.target: Das Essen war heute besonders gut.
example.en: The food was especially good today.

cards.trick: BeZONDers: something especially good stands out in a ZONE of its own.

example.target: Ich habe dir einen Brief geschrieben.

cards.trick: BRIEF sounds like "breef", just like English brief: a letter is often brief.
TIER sounds like "deer", and the two words share a root: a deer is an animal.

example.target: Pass auf, der Hund greift Fremde an!
example.en: Watch out, the dog attacks strangers!

cards.trick: ANGREIFEN sounds like AN-GRY-fen, and its past form angeGRIFFen sounds like griffin: picture an angry griffin swooping down to attack.

cards.hint: an exam, a test; the exact word, not schaffen
cards.trick: BESTEHEN sounds like "be-SHTAY-en": pass the test and you get to stay in the class.

example.target: Ich verstecke das Geschenk im Schrank.
example.en: I'm hiding the present in the wardrobe.

cards.trick: VERSTECKEN sounds like "fair-SHTECK-en": you STICK something away where nobody will look, so you hide it.

example.target: Der General gibt den Soldaten einen Befehl.
example.en: The general gives the soldiers an order.

cards.trick: GENERAL sounds like English general with a hard g and the stress on the end: geh-neh-RAHL, the officer in charge.
ABSOLUT sounds like English absolute said with a stressed LOOT at the end: an absolute haul of loot.
SICHERHEIT begins with SICHER, said ZISH-er, a bit like 'secure': Sicherheit is security and safety.
HEILIG starts with a sound like HIGH: holy things are high above us, up in heaven.
INTERESSANT sounds like "interesting" with the ending cut short to "ant": an interesting ant.

cards.hint: the basic verb, as in auf den Berg ___ or in den Bus ___; not klettern

example.target: Wir steigen morgen auf den Berg.

cards.trick: STEIGEN starts like "shtile", close to a stile, the steps you climb to get over a fence.

cards.hint: any room in a building, like a meeting room; not Zimmer

example.target: Der Raum ist zu klein für uns alle.
example.en: The room is too small for all of us.

cards.trick: RAUM sounds a lot like "room", just with an "ow" sound in the middle.
cards.why: Use Raum for any room in a building, like a meeting room; Zimmer for a room in a home or hotel.

cards.trick: BOSS is borrowed straight from English and sounds almost the same: the boss is the person in charge.
cards.why: Boss is casual, often for a gang or big shot; Chef is the usual word for your boss at work.

example.target: Ich brauche mehr Informationen über den Job.
example.en: I need more information about the job.

cards.trick: INFORMATION is spelled like the English word and means the same; just say the ending as in-for-ma-TSYOHN.

example.target: Ich will mit meinem Anwalt sprechen.
example.en: I want to talk to my lawyer.

cards.trick: ANWALT sounds like "an vault": a lawyer locks your secrets away in a vault.

cards.hint: keep someone safe from harm (the be- word, not schützen)
cards.trick: The middle of BESCHÜTZEN sounds a bit like shoots: a bodyguard shoots to protect you.
cards.why: Use beschützen for watching over a person; schützen for protecting in general, as from rain or cold.

example.target: Ich schwöre, ich war das nicht.

cards.trick: SCHWÖREN, said SHVUR-en, is a close cousin of English swear: picture raising your hand to swear an oath.

example.target: Der Ball rollt unter das Sofa.
example.en: The ball rolls under the sofa.

cards.trick: ROLLEN sounds almost like rolling, and rolling is just what a ball does.
VERRATEN has a rat in the middle: a rat is someone who gives away your secrets.

cards.hint: of a person, as in that's sweet of you; not nett, süß or freundlich

example.target: Das ist echt lieb von dir!

cards.trick: LIEB sounds like leap: a kind, sweet friend leaps up to help you.
cards.why: Use lieb for warm, affectionate sweetness; nett for plain friendliness and politeness.

cards.hint: mistaken; one reflexive verb, related to English err (not sich täuschen)
cards.trick: IRREN sounds like "err-en": to err is to be wrong, as in to err is human.
KÄMPFEN starts like KEMP, close to champ: a champ is someone who fights and wins.

example.target: Kannst du ein Geheimnis für dich behalten?

cards.trick: GeHEIMnis hides HEIM, said like hime and meaning home: a secret is something you keep at home and never tell.

cards.hint: someone in the act, a bus

example.target: Ich habe den Bus gerade noch erwischt.
example.en: I just barely caught the bus.

cards.trick: ERWISCHEN sounds like air-VISH-en, almost air fish: you catch a fish as it leaps into the air.
cards.why: Use erwischen for catching someone in the act or a bus; fangen for catching a ball or an animal.

cards.hint: make different, change how someone or something is (the ver- word, not ändern)
cards.trick: VERÄNDERN, said fair-EN-dern, sounds a bit like another: change something and it turns into another thing.
cards.why: Use verändern when something or someone really changes; use ändern to adjust a detail, like a plan or a time.

cards.hint: as in get into trouble; also anger
cards.trick: ÄRGER sounds like AIR-ger, close to anger: anger is what trouble brings.

cards.hint: for the first time, get to know

example.target: Heute lerne ich deine Eltern kennen.

cards.trick: KENNEN-LERNEN sounds like "ken" plus "learning": you learn someone into your ken when you first meet them.
cards.why: Use kennenlernen for meeting someone for the first time; treffen for meeting up with someone you already know.

cards.hint: keep someone from going on, also hold up or delay (not stoppen or anhalten)
cards.trick: AUF-HALTEN has HALT in it: you shout halt to stop someone and hold them back.
cards.why: Use aufhalten for stopping someone else; aufhören for stopping something you are doing.

cards.hint: informal, the same word as class
cards.trick: KLASSE sounds like classy: something classy is really great.

cards.hint: as in Are you mad at me? Not sauer or wütend

example.en: Are you still mad at me?

cards.trick: BÖSE sounds a little like bossy: a bossy boss gets angry at you all the time.
MEINUNG starts like MINE (MY-noong): your opinion is what's on your mind, it's yours alone.

cards.hint: mind or spirit as in zeitgeist, not a ghost, not Seele or Verstand

example.target: Im Geiste bin ich bei dir.

cards.trick: GEIST is the geist in zeitgeist, the spirit of the times.

example.en: We have to act fast now.

cards.trick: HANDELN sounds like handle: when trouble comes, you act and handle it.

cards.hint: also to ask a price, not fordern

example.target: Du verlangst zu viel von mir.
example.en: You're asking too much of me.

cards.trick: VerLANGen has lang in it, said like long: you demand the thing you long for.

example.target: Das Essen steht schon auf dem Tisch.
example.en: The food is already on the table.

cards.trick: TISCH sounds like dish: you put every dish on the table.
